_meta.descricao: Roman Pontiffs: apostolic succession and landmark pontificates.
_meta.aviso: This collection does not yet include the complete list of the Roman Pontiffs. For editorial use, always check the primary source cited in each entry.
_meta.revisao_editorial: For the pontificates of the first century there is no dating with documentary certainty; in these cases the date fields have been left null and the traditional information is stated as such in the body of the text.
fontes_gerais: vatican.va — archive of the Supreme Pontiffs

itens.resumo: Apostle chosen by Christ as the rock of the Church; first in the succession of the Bishops of Rome.
itens.corpo:
Simon, son of Jonah, a fisherman of Galilee, was called by Jesus and received from him the name Peter. The Gospels present him as the first among the Twelve; in Matthew 16:18-19 Christ declares to him: "You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my Church," entrusting to him the keys of the Kingdom.

The Acts of the Apostles recount his role in the first community of Jerusalem, at Pentecost, and in the opening of the preaching to the Gentiles. The tradition of the Church, attested since the first centuries, holds that Peter ended his ministry in Rome and there suffered martyrdom during the persecution of Nero, being buried on the Vatican hill, the site over which Saint Peter's Basilica was built.

There is no documentation that allows the dates of his pontificate to be fixed with certainty; for this reason this collection omits them. The First Vatican Council and the Second Vatican Council set forth the doctrine of the primacy of Peter and of his succession in the Bishops of Rome.
fontes: Mt 16:13-19; Jn 21:15-17; Acts of the Apostles 1-12
Second Vatican Council, Dogmatic Constitution "Lumen Gentium" (1964), nos. 18-23
Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 880-882

itens.resumo: Second Bishop of Rome in the succession of Peter, according to the list handed down by Saint Irenaeus of Lyon.
itens.corpo: Saint Irenaeus of Lyon, in the second century, and Eusebius of Caesarea, in the early fourth century, record Linus as the immediate successor of Peter at the head of the Church of Rome. Tradition, without contemporary documentation that would allow dates to be established precisely, places his governance in the decades following the martyrdom of Peter, under the emperors Vespasian and Titus. The Roman Canon of the Mass mentions him by name among the first apostolic successors.
fontes: Saint Irenaeus of Lyon, "Adversus Haereses" III, 3

itens.resumo: Third Bishop of Rome, successor of Linus; tradition attributes to him the ordination of presbyters for the Roman communities.
itens.corpo: Anacletus — also called Cletus in the oldest lists, forms of the same Greek name — succeeded Linus at the head of the Church of Rome at the end of the first century. The Liber Pontificalis attributes to him the ordination of twenty-five presbyters to serve the Christian communities then scattered throughout the city, one of the earliest signs of Roman clerical organization. Tradition counts him among the martyrs, though no reliable details of the circumstances are known.
itens.imagem_credito: Photo: Palma il Giovane (painting); Didier Descouens (photo) — Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0

itens.resumo: Fourth Bishop of Rome, author of the oldest known papal letter, addressed to the Church of Corinth.
itens.corpo: Clement is the first successor of Peter from whom a written work survives: the "Epistle to the Corinthians," composed around the year 96 to settle an internal dispute in that community, invoking the authority of apostolic succession to intervene in a church that was not his own. It is one of the oldest texts of Christian literature outside the New Testament and an early witness to the authority of the Bishop of Rome over other churches. Tradition places his martyrdom under Trajan.
fontes: Clement of Rome, "Epistle to the Corinthians" (c. 96)

itens.resumo: Pope of Jewish-Greek origin; tradition attributes to him the first division of Rome into parishes (titles).
itens.corpo: Son of a Greek father born in Antioch, according to the Liber Pontificalis, Evaristus governed the Church of Rome between the end of the pontificate of Clement I and the beginning of the second century. Tradition attributes to him the distribution of the city of Rome among presbyters responsible for local communities — the "titles," the embryo of the future parishes — and the institution of seven deacons to assist the bishop. He is venerated as a martyr.

itens.resumo: Sixth Bishop of Rome; later liturgical traditions associate his name with the blessing of water with salt used at Mass.
itens.corpo: Little is known with historical certainty about the pontificate of Alexander I, in the early second century. The Liber Pontificalis attributes to him the introduction of the use of holy water mixed with salt in the homes of the faithful and certain formulas of the Canon of the Mass — attributions that modern historical criticism considers later legends, and not a contemporary record. He is venerated as a martyr by the Roman tradition.

itens.resumo: Seventh Bishop of Rome; later liturgical traditions associate him with norms on the sacred vessels and with the singing of the Sanctus at Mass.
itens.corpo: A Roman by birth according to the Liber Pontificalis, Sixtus I governed the Church in the first quarter of the second century. Later sources attribute to him decrees reserving the touching of the sacred vessels to ordained ministers and the introduction of the "Sanctus" into the Eucharistic liturgy — traditions recorded centuries after his pontificate, not contemporary documents. He is venerated as a martyr.

itens.resumo: Greek pope of the second century; the only bishop of Rome of this period whose martyrdom is attested by a contemporary source, Saint Irenaeus.
itens.corpo: Of Greek origin, and probably a hermit before his election, Telesphorus is the first pope of this early period whose martyrdom is confirmed by a nearly contemporary witness: Saint Irenaeus of Lyon, writing a few decades later, expressly states that he "died gloriously for Christ." Later tradition attributes to him the institution of a period of fasting before Easter and of the nighttime celebration of Christmas, although these customs only became established at a later time.

itens.resumo: Greek pope of the mid-second century, a contemporary of the arrival in Rome of the first Gnostic teachers.
itens.corpo: A Greek philosopher by birth, according to the Liber Pontificalis, Hyginus governed the Church of Rome at a time when teachers associated with Gnostic currents — Valentinus and Cerdo among them — were arriving in the city and attracting followers. Tradition attributes to him some organization of the grades of the clergy, although no concrete decrees of his have been preserved. He is venerated as a martyr.

itens.resumo: Roman pope of the mid-second century; his pontificate saw the arrival in Rome of the heresy of Marcion.
itens.corpo: Brother of Hermas — author of the treatise «The Shepherd», one of the most widely read texts of the early Church outside the biblical canon —, Pius I governed the Church of Rome around 140-154. It was during his pontificate that Marcion, a merchant from Pontus who rejected the Old Testament and proposed a reduced canon of scriptures, arrived in Rome and was excluded from the communion of the Church. He is venerated as a martyr by tradition.

itens.resumo: Pope who received Saint Polycarp of Smyrna in Rome to discuss the date of Easter, in one of the best-documented meetings of the Church in the second century.
itens.corpo: A Syrian by birth, Anicetus governed the Church of Rome around 150-160. His pontificate is remembered above all for the visit of Polycarp of Smyrna, a disciple of the Apostle John, who came to Rome to discuss the divergence between East and West over the date of the celebration of Easter — the so-called Quartodeciman controversy. They did not reach an agreement, but, as Irenaeus of Lyons reports, they parted in communion and peace, with Anicetus yielding to Polycarp the honor of presiding at the Eucharist during his stay.
fontes: Irenaeus of Lyons, letter to Victor cited by Eusebius, "Ecclesiastical History" V, 24

itens.resumo: A pope remembered for his correspondence with the Church of Corinth and for his care for the confessors condemned to the mines.
itens.corpo: A native of Campania, Soter governed the Church of Rome in the second half of the 2nd century. He wrote to the Christian community of Corinth a letter now lost, mentioned with praise in a reply by Bishop Dionysius of Corinth—a testimony preserved by Eusebius of Caesarea—which highlights his charity toward the Christians condemned to forced labor in the mines because of their faith. He is venerated as a martyr.
fontes: Dionysius of Corinth, letter cited by Eusebius, "Ecclesiastical History" IV, 23

itens.resumo: Greek pope of the late second century; to him was attributed, in much later sources now considered legendary, the sending of missionaries to Britain.
itens.corpo: A Greek deacon native of Nicopolis before his election, Eleutherius governed the Church of Rome from approximately 175 to 189, a period marked by the spread of Gnostic currents and the rise of Montanism in Asia Minor. An eighth-century account, taken up by Bede the Venerable, attributes to him the sending of missionaries at the request of a supposed "King Lucius" of Britain — an episode that modern historiography considers a late legend, with no basis in any contemporary source, and which this collection records only as such.
fontes: Bede the Venerable, "Ecclesiastical History of the English People" I, 4 (late account)

itens.resumo: First pope of African origin; he demanded that the whole Church adopt the Western date of Easter, threatening with excommunication the churches of Asia Minor that resisted.
itens.corpo: A native of Roman Africa, Victor I was the first Bishop of Rome of that origin of whom we have certain knowledge. His pontificate, between 189 and 199, is marked by a firm resumption of the Quartodeciman controversy: unlike the conciliatory attitude of his predecessor Anicetus, Victor demanded that the churches of Asia Minor abandon their traditional date of Easter in favor of the Sunday observed in Rome, even threatening to cut them off from communion. Several bishops, among them Irenaeus of Lyon, interceded asking for moderation, and an open schism was avoided. He is venerated as a martyr.

itens.resumo: Pope of the early third century who faced the Monarchian controversies over the Trinity, with the deacon Callistus — a future pope — as a close adviser.
itens.corpo: A Roman by birth, Zephyrinus governed the Church from 199 to 217, a period of intense theological debate in Rome over how to reconcile the unity of God with the divinity of Christ — the so-called Monarchian currents, associated with names such as Praxeas and Sabellius. His chief adviser was the deacon Callistus, who was in charge of the Christian cemetery on the Appian Way and who would succeed him in the pontificate. The presbyter Hippolytus of Rome, a critic of both, is the main — hostile — source for this period.

itens.resumo: Pope of the early third century, associated with the Roman catacomb that bears his name and with debates over penitential discipline.
itens.corpo: A former slave, Callistus was a deacon in charge of the Christian cemetery on the Appian Way — today known as the Catacombs of Saint Callistus — before being elected Bishop of Rome around 217. His pontificate was marked by controversies with the presbyter Hippolytus, who accused him of excessive leniency in admitting to reconciliation penitents guilty of grave sins, such as adultery. Tradition counts him among the martyrs, a victim of a popular riot in Rome.
itens.imagem_credito: Photo: Hugo DK — Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0

itens.resumo: Roman pope of the early third century; the tradition of his martyrdom is now questioned, since the emperor of his time is known for his tolerance toward Christians.
itens.corpo: Roman by birth, Urban I succeeded Callixtus I at the head of the Church between 222 and 230, during the reign of Alexander Severus, an emperor recognized by historians for his relative religious tolerance, which has led modern scholars to question the tradition, recorded only in late sources, that Urban was martyred. Practically nothing else is known with certainty about his pontificate beyond what the Liber Pontificalis records.

itens.resumo: The first pope in history to resign from office, when he was deported with the antipope Hippolytus to the mines of Sardinia, where both died.
itens.corpo: Elected in 230, Pontian governed the Church of Rome until he was arrested and deported to the mines of Sardinia in 235, during the persecution launched by Emperor Maximinus Thrax — together with him was deported Hippolytus, a presbyter who had led a schism as a rival antipope since the pontificate of Callistus I. In the mines the two were reconciled before dying. To allow the election of a successor without an indefinite vacancy, Pontian formally resigned the pontificate on September 28, 235 — the first known case of papal resignation.

itens.resumo: Greek pope whose pontificate, among the shortest in history, lasted little more than a month.
itens.corpo: Of Greek origin, Anterus was elected in November 235, shortly after the deportation of Pontian to Sardinia, and died as early as January of the following year — one of the shortest pontificates ever recorded. The Liber Pontificalis attributes to him the care of gathering and preserving accounts of the Church's martyrs, although this attribution, like many from the period, is difficult to verify historically. He is venerated as a martyr.

itens.resumo: Pope elected in extraordinary circumstances according to Eusebius of Caesarea; he organized the administration of the Church of Rome and died at the beginning of the Decian persecution.
itens.corpo: A Roman layman who happened to be present at the assembly gathered to elect the new bishop, Fabian was singled out, according to the account of Eusebius of Caesarea, when a dove landed on his head — a sign that the assembly read as an indication of the Holy Spirit, electing him by acclamation even though he was not a cleric. He governed the Church from 236 to 250, dividing Rome into seven diaconal districts for the better administration of charity, and corresponded with Origen. He was one of the first victims of the persecution launched by the Emperor Decius, dying as a martyr in January 250.
fontes: Eusebius of Caesarea, "Ecclesiastical History" VI, 29 and 39

itens.resumo: Third-century pope who faced the schism of Novatian over the reconciliation of those who had apostatized under persecution.
itens.corpo: Elected in 251, shortly after the end of the persecution of Decius, Cornelius defended the possibility of reconciling the «lapsi» — Christians who had apostatized under torture — through penance, against the rigorist position of the presbyter Novatian, who had himself elected as a rival antipope. He had the support of Saint Cyprian of Carthage in this controversy, recorded in correspondence that survives to this day. He died in exile during the persecution of Gallus, and is venerated as a martyr.
itens.imagem_credito: Photo: Hugo DK — Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0
fontes: Correspondence between Cornelius and Saint Cyprian of Carthage

itens.resumo: Roman pope with a brief pontificate, exiled shortly after his election and who died soon after being able to return to Rome.
itens.corpo: Elected in 253, Lucius I was almost immediately exiled by Emperor Trebonianus Gallus, at a time of renewed hostility against Christians. He was able to return to Rome shortly afterward, but died only a few months later, in 254. Saint Cyprian of Carthage, a correspondent of the Roman See during this period, praised his steadfastness in the face of exile.

itens.resumo: Pope involved in a controversy with Cyprian of Carthage over the validity of baptism administered by heretics — a position that prevailed in the doctrine of the Church.
itens.corpo: Stephen I governed the Church of Rome from 254 to 257, a period in which an important dispute arose with Cyprian of Carthage and the African bishops: they maintained that baptism administered by heretics and schismatics was invalid and had to be repeated; Stephen held that baptism was valid as long as it was performed with water and in the Trinitarian formula, regardless of who administered it, the laying on of hands being sufficient to reconcile the convert. The correspondence between the two, preserved by Cyprian, is one of the richest sources on the ecclesiology of the third century. Stephen's position would prevail as the doctrine of the Church.

itens.resumo: Pope martyred during the persecution of Valerian, surprised while celebrating the liturgy in a Roman catacomb.
itens.corpo: Elected in 257, Sixtus II governed the Church at a time of renewed persecution under Emperor Valerian, whose edict of 258 ordered the immediate execution of bishops, priests, and deacons. He was surprised while presiding at a celebration in the Catacomb of Praetextatus in Rome, and was beheaded on the spot together with four deacons. His deacon Lawrence, who was in charge of administering the Church's goods, would be martyred a few days later, an episode that would become one of the most celebrated in the Roman martyrial tradition.

itens.resumo: Pope elected after a long vacancy caused by the persecution of Valerian; he intervened in a theological dispute with Dionysius of Alexandria.
itens.corpo: The death of Sixtus II during the persecution left the See of Rome vacant for almost a year, until the end of the persecution, with the capture of Valerian in 260, allowed a regular election. Dionysius, elected in 259, devoted himself to reorganizing the Roman Church and to distributing responsibilities among the urban parishes. He also intervened in a theological controversy with his namesake Dionysius, Bishop of Alexandria, who was challenged over formulations that seemed to come close to Sabellianism in treating the distinction between the Father and the Son.
fontes: Athanasius of Alexandria, "On the Decrees of the Council of Nicaea" 26

itens.resumo: Pope of the second half of the third century about whose pontificate almost nothing is known with historical certainty beyond the record of the Liber Pontificalis.
itens.corpo: Successor of Dionysius, Felix I governed the Church of Rome from 269 to 274, during a period of relative respite between the great persecutions. Little concrete is known about his pontificate; later tradition venerates him as a martyr, an attribution that historical criticism considers uncertain, possibly the result of confusion with another Christian of the same name buried in the Roman catacombs.

itens.resumo: Pope of the second half of the third century, a period of relative peace for the Church between two great waves of persecution.
itens.corpo: Eutychian governed the Church of Rome between 275 and 283, in a time of relative tolerance that followed the end of the persecutions of Valerian and Aurelian. The Liber Pontificalis attributes to him numerous burials of martyrs in the Roman catacombs, information that is difficult to verify with historical precision. Almost nothing else is known for certain about his governance.

itens.resumo: Pope whose pontificate ended shortly before the start of the Great Persecution of Diocletian, the most severe waged against Christians.
itens.corpo: Caius governed the Church of Rome from 283 to 296. Late sources of questionable reliability associate him with the family of the Emperor Diocletian, although this relationship cannot be confirmed by contemporary documentation. He died before 303, the year in which Diocletian would unleash the most systematic and violent persecution against Christians in the entire history of the Roman Empire.

itens.resumo: Pope whose pontificate coincided with the beginning of Diocletian's Great Persecution; controversial traditions, now disputed, claim a temporary apostasy.
itens.corpo: Marcellinus was elected in 296 and was governing the Church when, in 303, Diocletian unleashed the most violent persecution ever waged against Christians, with orders to destroy churches, burn the Scriptures, and imprison the clergy. Hostile sources from the Donatist movement, written decades later, went so far as to claim that Marcellinus had handed over sacred books to the authorities to save his life — an accusation that historical criticism regards as late propaganda, with no confirmation in any reliable contemporary source. He died in 304, probably a victim of the persecution itself.
fontes: Augustine of Hippo, "Against the Letter of Parmenian" (refutation of the Donatist accusation)

itens.resumo: Pope elected after four years of vacancy caused by persecution; exiled by Maxentius amid disturbances over the reconciliation of those who had apostatized.
itens.corpo: The death of Marcellinus in the midst of persecution left the See of Rome vacant for about four years, until Marcellus could be elected in 308. His pontificate immediately faced the problem of how to readmit to communion the «lapsi» who had yielded during the persecution — a question that divided the Roman community and led to public riots. Emperor Maxentius, claiming the need to restore order, exiled Marcellus from Rome, where he would die shortly afterward, in 309.

itens.resumo: Pope whose pontificate was extremely brief, also exiled by Maxentius amid the same dispute over the reconciliation of apostates.
itens.corpo: Successor of Marcellus, Eusebius governed for a few months in 309, continuing the dispute over the treatment of the «lapsi», this time facing opposition from a presbyter named Heraclius, who defended stricter criteria for reconciliation. Like his predecessor, he was exiled by order of Maxentius — to Sicily, according to tradition —, where he died that same year.
fontes: Funerary inscription of Saint Damasus I (Damasi Epigrammata)

itens.resumo: Pope who witnessed the end of the persecutions and the Edict of Milan; he received from Constantine the Lateran Palace, the future seat of the popes.
itens.corpo: Elected in 311, Miltiades presided over the Church of Rome at exactly the moment of the decisive turning point in its history: in 313, Emperor Constantine, together with Licinius, promulgated the Edict of Milan, granting freedom of worship to Christians after centuries of intermittent persecution. Constantine donated the Lateran Palace to the Church of Rome, and it would become the papal residence for almost a thousand years. Also in 313, Miltiades presided in Rome over a synod that examined the case of Bishop Caecilian of Carthage, who was contested by what would become the Donatist schism in North Africa.
fontes: Acts of the Synod of Rome (313)

itens.resumo: A pope contemporary with the Constantinian basilicas and the Council of Nicaea; the Middle Ages falsely attributed to him the "Donation of Constantine."
itens.corpo:
One of the longest and most historically significant pontificates of the early centuries, that of Sylvester I (314-336) coincided with the construction, sponsored by Constantine, of the first great Christian basilicas of Rome — Saint John Lateran, Saint Peter's in the Vatican, and others. In 325 the first ecumenical council in history met at Nicaea, convened by Constantine to respond to the Arian crisis; Sylvester did not attend in person, but sent legates who signed in his name.

Centuries after his death, a forged document known as the "Donation of Constantine" began to circulate, attributing to Sylvester the miraculous cure of Constantine's supposed leprosy and claiming that the emperor had donated to him temporal authority over the West. Historical criticism conclusively demonstrated, as early as the Renaissance, that the document is an eighth-century forgery — none of these stories has any basis in a source contemporary with Sylvester.
fontes: Acts of the First Council of Nicaea (325)

itens.resumo: Pope of a brief pontificate; tradition attributes to him the norm that the Bishop of Ostia consecrate new popes.
itens.corpo: Mark succeeded Sylvester I in January 336, governing the Church for less than a year. Tradition attributes to him the building of two basilicas in Rome and the establishment of the custom, maintained for centuries, that the episcopal consecration of a new pope be conferred by the Bishop of Ostia.

itens.resumo: Pope who defended Athanasius of Alexandria against his Arian accusers and asserted the authority of Rome to review the deposition of bishops of other sees.
itens.corpo: Julius I governed the Church of Rome from 337 to 352, in a period of intense turmoil caused by the Arian controversy. He welcomed to Rome Bishop Athanasius of Alexandria, who had been deposed and exiled under pressure from bishops of Arian orientation, and convened a synod in 340-341 that declared him innocent of the accusations raised against him. In doing so, Julius affirmed the principle that the deposition of a bishop by a provincial council could be reviewed by the See of Rome — a milestone in the assertion of Roman authority over the wider Church, later confirmed by the canons of the Council of Sardica (343).
fontes: Canons of the Council of Sardica (343)

itens.resumo: A pope exiled for defending Athanasius against the Arian emperor Constantius II; historians still debate how much he conceded in order to return from exile.
itens.corpo:
Elected in 352, Liberius at first maintained his defense of Athanasius of Alexandria against the pressure of Emperor Constantius II, who was of Arian conviction, refusing to sign his condemnation. For this reason he was exiled to Thrace in 355, while Rome saw the installation of an antipope, Felix II, supported by the imperial court.

Tradition — whose exact extent is now debated — reports that Liberius, under the pressure of exile, signed some compromise formula of Semi-Arian tendency in order to obtain permission to return to Rome in 358. The real extent of this concession is still debated by historians, because fully reliable sources on the episode are lacking; because of this controversy, Liberius is the first pope whom the later Western tradition ceased to venerate universally as a saint.
fontes: Athanasius of Alexandria, "History of the Arians"

itens.resumo: Fourth-century pope who commissioned Saint Jerome to produce the Bible translation that would become the Latin Vulgate.
itens.corpo: Bishop of Rome from 366 to 384, Damasus I presided over the Council of Rome of 382, which produced one of the earliest known lists of the canonical books of Scripture. It was he who charged his secretary, Jerome, with revising and translating the biblical texts into a Latin more faithful to the originals, a work that would result, over the course of decades, in the Vulgate. He also promoted the veneration of the Roman martyrs, restoring and marking their tombs in the catacombs with poetic inscriptions of his own composition.
fontes: Saint Jerome, correspondence with Damasus I

itens.resumo: The first pope to write a decretal in the legal sense of the term — the oldest surviving papal legislative document.
itens.corpo: Siricius governed the Church of Rome from 384 to 399. His "Decretal to Himerius of Tarragona," of 385, is the oldest document of this genre to have survived to the present day: written in the tone of ecclesiastical law, and not of a simple pastoral letter, it dealt with clerical discipline — among other points, the celibacy of priests and deacons who were married before ordination — and with the reconciliation of penitents. The document is a landmark in the assertion of the normative authority of the Bishop of Rome over the whole Western Church.

itens.resumo: Pope who condemned the writings of Origen, praised by Saint Jerome and Saint Augustine for his pastoral zeal.
itens.corpo: Anastasius I governed the Church from 399 to 401, a period in which the controversy over the orthodoxy of the writings of Origen, a third-century theologian whose speculations were then being challenged by Jerome and Theophilus of Alexandria, was intensifying. Anastasius formally condemned the writings considered problematic, without extending the condemnation to the person of Origen. Saint Jerome and Saint Augustine, both his contemporaries, left laudatory records of his pastoral conduct.

itens.resumo: Pope who asserted Roman primacy, witnessed the sack of Rome by the Visigoths, and condemned Pelagianism at the request of Augustine and the African bishops.
itens.corpo:
Innocent I governed the Church from 401 to 417, a period of intense affirmation of Rome's doctrinal and disciplinary authority: he maintained that no important ecclesiastical question should be decided without recourse to the Roman See. He was absent from Rome, in Ravenna, negotiating with Emperor Honorius, when the city was sacked by Alaric's Visigoths in 410 — one of the most traumatic episodes of the end of the Western Roman Empire.

At the request of the African councils led by Saint Augustine of Hippo, he formally condemned the teachings of Pelagius and Caelestius on grace and free will, endorsing the conclusions of the African bishops — an episode that gave rise to the famous later expression «Roma locuta, causa finita» («Rome has spoken, the case is closed»).

itens.resumo: Greek pope who initially inclined toward accepting the orthodoxy of Pelagius and Caelestius, reversing his position under pressure from the African bishops.
itens.corpo: Of Greek origin, Zosimus governed for a little over a year, between 417 and 418. Upon taking office, he reviewed the case of Caelestius and Pelagius, who had already been condemned by his predecessor Innocent I, and for a time was inclined to consider them orthodox, on the basis of new professions of faith they presented. The vigorous reaction of the African bishops, gathered in council at Carthage in 418 under the leadership of Saint Augustine, led Zosimus to reverse his initial position and confirm the condemnation of Pelagianism before dying that same year.
fontes: Augustine of Hippo, "Against Two Letters of the Pelagians"

itens.resumo: Pope whose election was contested by a rival antipope, a dispute resolved by Emperor Honorius's intervention in his favor.
itens.corpo: The election of Boniface I, in 418, was immediately contested by the faction that had elected Eulalius as bishop of Rome, producing a schism that required the intervention of Emperor Honorius, who, after initial hesitation, decided in favor of Boniface and exiled Eulalius. Once settled in office, Boniface continued the line of his predecessors in asserting Rome's authority over the metropolitan sees and reinforced decrees on clerical discipline.
fontes: Imperial constitution of Honorius on the electoral dispute (419)

itens.resumo: Pope under whose authority the Council of Ephesus condemned Nestorianism and proclaimed Mary as Mother of God.
itens.corpo: Celestine I governed the Church from 422 to 432. Faced with the teaching of Nestorius, Patriarch of Constantinople, who resisted calling Mary «Theotokos» (Mother of God) on the grounds that it would confuse the human and divine natures of Christ, Celestine commissioned Cyril of Alexandria to act in his name against Nestorius. The Council of Ephesus, the third ecumenical council, convened in 431 under this authority, condemned Nestorianism and solemnly confirmed Mary's title as Mother of God. Celestine also sent Bishop Palladius as a missionary to the Christians of Ireland, one of the earliest records of organized Roman missionary activity on that island.
fontes: Acts of the Council of Ephesus (431)

itens.resumo: Pope who worked for reconciliation after the Council of Ephesus and had the Basilica of Saint Mary Major built in Rome.
itens.corpo: Sixtus III succeeded Celestine I in 432, inheriting the tensions left by the Council of Ephesus between the supporters of Cyril of Alexandria and those of John of Antioch. He worked for reconciliation between the two parties, contributing to the "Formula of Union of 433" between Cyril and John. In Rome, he had the Basilica of Saint Mary Major built, whose triumphal arch mosaics celebrate precisely the proclamation of Mary as Mother of God made at Ephesus — one of the most important artistic monuments of the early Christian era that survive to this day.
fontes: Inscriptions on the triumphal arch of Saint Mary Major

itens.resumo: Fifth-century pope, author of the «Tome to Flavian» that guided the Christological definition of the Council of Chalcedon.
itens.corpo: Leo I, Bishop of Rome from 440 to 461, is one of the most influential figures in the history of the early papacy. His «Tome to Flavian» (449), setting out the doctrine of the two natures — divine and human — united in the one person of Christ, was read at the Council of Chalcedon (451) and received by the council fathers with the acclamation «Peter has spoken through Leo». He is also remembered for having gone in person to meet Attila the Hun in 452, persuading him not to advance on Rome. He was proclaimed a Doctor of the Church.
fontes: Saint Leo the Great, «Tome to Flavian» (449)
Acts of the Council of Chalcedon (451)

itens.resumo: A pope who, as a legate, narrowly escaped the tumultuous 'Robber Synod' of Ephesus; as Bishop of Rome, he reinforced norms on episcopal succession.
itens.corpo: Before being elected pope, Hilarius had taken part in 449, as legate of the then Pope Leo the Great, in the Council of Ephesus that history would christen the «Robber Council» («robbery», in reference to the violence and irregular maneuvers that marked it) — escaping from there with difficulty. Elected Bishop of Rome in 461, he convened a synod in 465 that produced important decrees on the order of episcopal succession and on clerical discipline, among the oldest conciliar records preserved in full in the West.

itens.resumo: The pope whose pontificate witnessed the fall of the Western Roman Empire in 476.
itens.corpo: Simplicius governed the Church of Rome from 468 to 483, a period that saw the end of the Western Roman Empire: in 476, the Germanic general Odoacer deposed the last Western emperor, Romulus Augustulus, a landmark traditionally used to date the end of Antiquity in the West. In this context of political collapse, the Church of Rome was consolidating itself as an institution of continuity. In the East, Simplicius followed with growing concern the Christological tensions that, under his successors, would lead to the Acacian Schism with Constantinople.

itens.resumo: Pope who excommunicated the Patriarch of Constantinople over a Christological compromise formula, opening the Acacian Schism between Rome and the East.
itens.corpo: Felix III governed the Church from 483 to 492. His pontificate is marked by the break with Acacius, Patriarch of Constantinople, who had subscribed to the «Henotikon», a compromise formula promoted by Emperor Zeno to pacify Chalcedonians and Monophysites, but which, in the eyes of Rome, yielded too much ground to Monophysite positions by avoiding a clear reaffirmation of the Council of Chalcedon. Felix excommunicated Acacius in 484, beginning the Acacian Schism, which would separate Rome and Constantinople for 35 years.

itens.resumo: Fifth-century pope, formulator of the doctrine of the "two swords" on the relationship between spiritual and temporal authority.
itens.corpo: Bishop of Rome from 492 to 496, Gelasius I is remembered above all for his letter to the Byzantine emperor Anastasius I, in which he distinguishes the "sacred authority of the pontiffs" from the "royal power," affirming that, in matters of faith, the emperor must submit to the bishops. This formulation would exert a lasting influence on medieval political theory concerning the relationship between Church and State. He is also associated with the establishment of the "Gelasian Decree" (Decretum Gelasianum), an ancient list of accepted and apocryphal books.
fontes: Saint Gelasius I, Letter to Emperor Anastasius I (494)

itens.resumo: Pope who tried to bring Rome and Constantinople closer together during the Acacian Schism, a conciliatory stance that divided the Roman clergy.
itens.corpo: Anastasius II governed for just over two years, from 496 to 498, seeking a path of reconciliation with Constantinople in the Acacian Schism, which had been opened decades earlier under Felix III. His willingness to treat the memory of the late Patriarch Acacius with leniency divided the Roman clergy between those who approved of the diplomatic path and those who saw it as an excessive concession. A late medieval legend — with no solid historical basis, and therefore recorded here only as such — went so far as to attribute his death to divine punishment; Dante Alighieri, following this legendary tradition, placed him among the heretics in the "Inferno" of the Divine Comedy.

itens.resumo: Pope whose disputed election gave rise to a schism lasting several years, resolved through the arbitration of the Ostrogothic king Theodoric.
itens.corpo: The election of Symmachus, in 498, was contested by a faction that simultaneously elected the archdeacon Laurentius, beginning what is known as the Laurentian Schism. The Ostrogothic king Theodoric, although an Arian, was called upon to arbitrate the dispute as the political authority of Rome and initially decided in favor of Symmachus, because he had been elected first and by a majority. The schism, however, dragged on for years, with mutual accusations of misconduct, until successive synods definitively confirmed Symmachus as the legitimate pope.
itens.imagem_credito: Photo: José Luiz — Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0
fontes: Ennodius of Pavia, "Apologetic in Defense of the Synod"

itens.resumo: Pope who ended the 35 years of the Acacian Schism, obtaining from the Eastern bishops their signature to a formula reaffirming Chalcedon and the primacy of Rome.
itens.corpo: Hormisdas governed the Church from 514 to 523, achieving what several of his predecessors had sought without success: the end of the Acacian Schism. In 519, with the support of the new Byzantine emperor Justin I — who broke with his predecessors' conciliatory policy toward Monophysitism —, he obtained the signature of the patriarch and the bishops of Constantinople to the so-called "Formula of Hormisdas," a document that solemnly reaffirmed the Council of Chalcedon and acknowledged that the See of Rome had never departed from the true faith. The text would remain a reference in Catholic ecclesiology on Petrine primacy.

itens.resumo: Pope sent on a diplomatic mission to Constantinople by the Arian king Theodoric; he died in prison, under suspicion of disloyalty upon his return.
itens.corpo: Elected in 523, John I was sent by the Ostrogothic king Theodoric — an Arian by faith, but until then tolerant toward the Catholics of Italy — on a delegation to Constantinople, to ask Emperor Justin I to soften recent measures against the Arians of the East, in reciprocity for the tolerance that Catholics enjoyed under Gothic rule. The embassy was received with great honors in Constantinople, which aroused Theodoric's suspicion: upon his return, John was imprisoned in Ravenna on suspicion of collusion with the Byzantine emperor, and died in prison in 526. He is venerated as a martyr.

itens.resumo: Pope appointed under the strong influence of the Ostrogothic king Athalaric; he had the basilica of Saints Cosmas and Damian built in the Roman Forum.
itens.corpo: The election of Felix IV, in 526, was marked by explicit pressure from the Ostrogothic court, then under the regency that was preparing the succession of Theodoric by the young Athalaric. During his pontificate he converted two ancient buildings of the Roman Forum into a Christian basilica, dedicating it to the holy physicians Cosmas and Damian — a church whose apse mosaics, with Felix himself depicted, survive to this day as one of the best-preserved ensembles of sixth-century Christian art.
fontes: Inscriptions of the Basilica of Saints Cosmas and Damian

itens.resumo: First pope of Germanic descent; he tried to name his own successor by decree, a practice he himself had to revoke under protest from the Roman clergy.
itens.corpo: Boniface II, from an Ostrogothic family, governed between 530 and 532, and was the first pope of Germanic origin of whom we have record. He attempted to establish, by decree, that the deacon Vigilius would be his automatic successor — a precedent with no basis in the elective tradition of the Roman Church, which provoked a strong reaction from the clergy. Faced with opposition, Boniface was forced to publicly burn his own decree at a synod, reversing the measure before his death.
fontes: Acts of the Roman Synod (531) on the revocation of the decree

itens.resumo: First pope to adopt a new name upon his election, because his baptismal name, Mercurius, referred to a pagan deity.
itens.corpo: Elected in 533, the new pope was baptized Mercurius, the name of a deity of Roman mythology considered unsuitable for the head of the Church; for this reason, he took the name John, becoming the first pontiff in history to change his name upon assuming the office, a practice that, centuries later, would become a universal custom among the popes. He received from the Ostrogothic king Athalaric confirmation that the papal election, although subject to royal approval, should not involve simony.
fontes: Edict of Athalaric on the papal election (533)

itens.resumo: Pope who traveled to Constantinople to negotiate peace between the Ostrogoths and the Byzantines on the eve of the Gothic War, and who there deposed a patriarch with Monophysite leanings.
itens.corpo: Agapetus I governed for slightly less than a year, between 535 and 536, but his brief pontificate had considerable historical weight: sent by the Ostrogothic king Theodahad to Constantinople to try to avert the war that Emperor Justinian was preparing against the Ostrogothic kingdom of Italy, he was unable to prevent the conflict — the beginning of the long and destructive Gothic War — but, once in the Byzantine capital, he obtained the deposition of Patriarch Anthimus I, who had Monophysite leanings. He died in Constantinople before he could return to Rome.

itens.resumo: Son of Pope Hormisdas; deposed by the Byzantine general Belisarius under pressure from Empress Theodora and sent into exile, he died shortly afterward in obscure circumstances.
itens.corpo: Son of Pope Hormisdas — born before his father's ordination, at a time when clerical celibacy was not yet observed with the rigor of later centuries —, Silverius was installed as pope in 536 with the support of the Ostrogothic king Theodahad, already in the midst of the Gothic War. When the Byzantine troops of General Belisarius took Rome, Empress Theodora, who wanted a pope more favorable to her Monophysite sympathies, pressed for his deposition on a forged charge of treason. Silverius was exiled and died shortly afterward, in 537, in circumstances that tradition attributes to mistreatment — and for this reason he is venerated as a martyr.

itens.resumo: Pope installed with Byzantine support after the deposition of Silverius; he spent years in custody in Constantinople amid the Three Chapters Controversy.
itens.corpo:
Vigilius assumed the pontificate in 537 with the backing of the Byzantine court, after the removal of Silverius. His reign was marked by the so-called Three Chapters Controversy: pressured by Emperor Justinian to condemn writings of three authors linked to the Antiochene tradition — seen by Justinian as an obstacle to reconciliation with the Monophysites —, Vigilius wavered, at times yielding, at times retreating in the face of resistance from Western bishops who feared an implicit condemnation of the Council of Chalcedon.

Brought by force to Constantinople in 545, he remained there in custody for almost eight years, at one point taking refuge in a church to escape physical arrest. He ended up accepting the conclusions of the Second Council of Constantinople (553), which condemned the Three Chapters, but he died in 555 on the journey back to Rome, never having returned to the city.
fontes: Acts of the Second Council of Constantinople (553)

itens.resumo: Pope who inherited the division of the West over the condemnation of the Three Chapters, while Rome was recovering from the years of devastation of the Gothic War.
itens.corpo: Successor of Vigilius, Pelagius I governed between 556 and 561, a period in which a good part of the West — especially northern Italy and Roman Africa — refused to accept the condemnation of the Three Chapters confirmed at the Second Council of Constantinople, fearing that it would weaken the authority of Chalcedon. This disagreement would give rise to the so-called Schism of the Three Chapters, which would persist in some regions for more than a century. Pelagius also devoted himself to the reconstruction of Rome, devastated by almost two decades of the Gothic War.
fontes: Letters of Pelagius I to the Western bishops

itens.resumo: Pope whose pontificate saw the beginning of the Lombard invasion of Italy, relying on the Byzantine general Narses for the defense of the region.
itens.corpo: John III governed the Church from 561 to 574, precisely at the moment when the Lombards, a Germanic people from the north, invaded Italy in 568, beginning an occupation that would fragment the peninsula for centuries. He had the support of the Byzantine general Narses, then governing the Italy reconquered by Justinian, in trying to contain the Lombard advance — though without lasting success.
fontes: Paul the Deacon, "History of the Lombards"

itens.resumo: Pope whose pontificate unfolded entirely under the siege and famine caused by the Lombard invasion of Rome.
itens.corpo: Benedict I governed the Church from 575 to 579, a period of great suffering for Rome, surrounded and isolated by the Lombard armies that already controlled a good part of Italy. The sources of the period record severe famine in the city. Little else is known with certainty about his pontificate, which was marked above all by the survival of the Roman community in extreme conditions.
fontes: Gregory of Tours, "History of the Franks"

itens.resumo: Pope who sent the future Saint Gregory the Great as ambassador to Constantinople; he died a victim of the plague that ravaged Rome in 590.
itens.corpo: Pelagius II governed from 579 to 590, continuing to face the Lombard threat to Rome and seeking, without great success, the help of the Frankish kings against the Germanic advance. He raised the deacon Gregory — who would be his successor under the name Gregory the Great — to the office of apocrisiarius, the permanent papal representative at the imperial court in Constantinople, a post of great diplomatic importance. He died in 590, a victim of a plague epidemic that devastated Rome that year.
fontes: Gregory of Tours, "History of the Franks"

itens.resumo: Pope of the sixth century, Doctor of the Church, organizer of the Roman liturgy and patron of the evangelizing mission to England.
itens.corpo: A former prefect of Rome who became a Benedictine monk, Gregory I was elected pope in 590, amid the crisis caused by the Lombard invasions and the collapse of the administrative structures of the former Western Roman Empire. He reorganized the administration of the papal estates in order to aid the poor of Rome, consolidated liturgical and sacred chant practices that later tradition would name "Gregorian chant," and sent the monk Augustine of Canterbury to evangelize Anglo-Saxon England in 596. His work "Pastoral Rule" became a reference for bishops for centuries. He is venerated as a Doctor of the Church.
fontes: Bede the Venerable, "Ecclesiastical History of the English People"

itens.resumo: Successor of Saint Gregory the Great, his pontificate was overshadowed in popular memory by comparison with his predecessor.
itens.corpo: Sabinian succeeded Gregory the Great in 604, inheriting a Church of Rome that his predecessor had left reorganized and recognized for its action in the face of famine and war. Later tradition, possibly exaggerated, accuses him of having managed the Church's grain reserves more strictly during a period of scarcity — a deliberate contrast, in the sources, with the generosity attributed to Gregory. Little else is known with certainty about his brief government.
fontes: John the Deacon, «Life of Saint Gregory the Great» (comparative mention)

itens.resumo: Pope with a very brief pontificate who obtained from Emperor Phocas the recognition of the See of Rome as the head of all the churches.
itens.corpo: Boniface III governed for less than a year, in 607, but obtained from the Byzantine Emperor Phocas a decree of great symbolic weight: the formal recognition that the Bishop of Rome was the "head of all the Churches," in opposition to the claim of the Patriarch of Constantinople to use the title of "Ecumenical Patriarch" — a dispute over precedence that had already dragged on for decades between the two sees.

itens.resumo: Pope who converted the Pantheon of Rome into a Christian church, a gesture that ensured the monument's survival to this day.
itens.corpo: Boniface IV, a former Benedictine monk, governed between 608 and 615. He obtained from Emperor Phocas the gift of the Pantheon — the great pagan temple built centuries earlier in honor of all the Roman gods — and consecrated it as a Christian church dedicated to Saint Mary and all the martyrs, under the name of Santa Maria ad Martyres. This gesture is the main reason why the Pantheon, unlike so many other monuments of ancient Rome, remains practically intact to this day, being the best-preserved Roman building of Antiquity.
fontes: Bede the Venerable, «Ecclesiastical History of the English People» II, 4

itens.resumo: Pope of the early seventh century about whose pontificate few detailed records remain apart from the Liber Pontificalis.
itens.corpo: Adeodatus I, also referred to in some sources as Deusdedit, governed the Church of Rome from 615 to 618. The Liber Pontificalis highlights his pastoral dedication to the Roman clergy and a particular care for the lepers of the city, but little else is known with certainty about his pontificate.

itens.resumo: Pope who defended the right of ecclesiastical asylum and supported the young mission to evangelize Anglo-Saxon England.
itens.corpo: Boniface V governed between 619 and 625, a period in which he legally reinforced the right of asylum in churches, protecting from persecution those who sought refuge there. He corresponded with the missionaries who were continuing in England the evangelization begun by order of Gregory the Great decades earlier, writing letters of encouragement to King Edwin of Northumbria and his court — episodes recorded in detail by the English monk Bede the Venerable.
fontes: Bede the Venerable, "Ecclesiastical History of the English People" II, 7-11

itens.resumo: Pope whose letters on the will of Christ were posthumously condemned by the Third Council of Constantinople — a central case in the debate over the papal magisterium.
itens.corpo:
Honorius I governed from 625 to 638. Faced with the Monothelite controversy — which sought to reconcile the Chalcedonians and the Monophysites by proposing that Christ, despite having two natures, had only one will — he answered inquiries from Patriarch Sergius of Constantinople in terms that seemed to favor this formula, which is now considered incompatible with the full humanity of Christ.

Forty years after his death, the Third Council of Constantinople (680-681) condemned Monothelitism and, along with it, anathematized Honorius by name for his letters — one of the very rare cases in history in which an ecumenical council posthumously condemns a pope. The episode is frequently discussed in theological debates about the limits of the papal magisterium, since it concerned private correspondence on a question not yet defined by the Church, and not a solemn definition of faith.
itens.imagem_credito: Photo: José Luiz — Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0
fontes: Acts of the Third Council of Constantinople (680-681)
Letters of Honorius I to Sergius of Constantinople

itens.resumo: Pope whose consecration was delayed for almost two years by political disputes over Monothelitism, dying only a few months after finally taking office.
itens.corpo: Elected in 638, Severinus could only be consecrated almost two years later, in 640, because the Byzantine government in Ravenna made its approval conditional on his acceptance of the «Ecthesis», an imperial edict that imposed the Monothelite formula as a way of ending the Christological controversy. Severinus resisted this pressure. Once consecrated, he governed for less than two months before dying.

itens.resumo: Pope who formally condemned Monothelitism and sought to defend the memory of Honorius I, claiming that his words had been misinterpreted.
itens.corpo: John IV, of Dalmatian origin, governed between 640 and 642. He convened a synod in Rome that explicitly condemned Monothelitism, and wrote in defense of the memory of his predecessor Honorius I, arguing that Honorius had intended only to deny that there were in Christ two wills contradicting each other, not the existence of a human will distinct from the divine — a defense that most historians consider insufficient in light of the actual content of Honorius's letters. John IV also worked to ransom Christians from Dalmatia captured in Slavic raids.
fontes: John IV, apologetic letter on Honorius I

itens.resumo: Pope of Greek origin who maintained firm opposition to Monothelitism, even going so far as to excommunicate the Patriarch of Constantinople.
itens.corpo: A native of Palestine, of Greek family, Theodore I governed from 642 to 649, continuing Rome's firm rejection of Monothelitism. He excommunicated Patriarch Paul II of Constantinople for supporting the «Typos», a new imperial edict that attempted to end the controversy simply by forbidding any public discussion of the subject — a measure that Rome regarded as a way of imposing silence on an error instead of correcting it.
fontes: Acts of the Lateran Council (649, convened under his successor)

itens.resumo: Pope imprisoned by the Byzantine emperor for condemning Monothelitism without imperial authorization, exiled and killed by mistreatment — the last pope venerated as a martyr.
itens.corpo:
Martin I was elected in 649 and, without waiting for the customary confirmation of the Byzantine exarch of Ravenna, immediately convened the Lateran Council of that same year, which solemnly condemned Monothelitism and the «Typos» that sought to impose silence on the question. The reaction of Emperor Constans II was violent: in 653, Martin was forcibly arrested in Rome, taken under guard to Constantinople, subjected to a humiliating trial in a public square and, finally, exiled to Cherson, in Crimea.

The letters he wrote from there, describing the privations and mistreatment he suffered, have survived and are one of the most moving testimonies of ancient papal history. He died in exile in 655, being the last pope venerated by tradition as a martyr for direct persecution by a political power.
fontes: Letters of Saint Martin I written in exile

itens.resumo: Pope elected while his predecessor Martin I was still living in exile, in a delicate situation that reflected the climate of imperial persecution of the papacy.
itens.corpo: Eugene I was elected in 654, while Martin I was still alive, imprisoned in exile in the Crimea and unable to exercise his office — a juridically delicate situation that the Church had to manage with caution in the face of the persecution waged by the Emperor Constans II. With the prudence required by the political circumstances, he maintained the opposition to Monothelitism inherited from his predecessors.

itens.resumo: Pope who received the Byzantine emperor Constans II in Rome and appointed Theodore of Tarsus Archbishop of Canterbury, a decisive choice for the English Church.
itens.corpo: Vitalian governed between 657 and 672, seeking to reduce tensions with Constantinople after years of persecution of the papacy over Monothelitism. In 663 he received in Rome a visit from the emperor Constans II himself — an episode marked, according to the chroniclers, by the removal of various bronze elements from Roman monuments, including the roof of the Pantheon, to be taken to Constantinople. Vitalian also appointed the Greek monk Theodore of Tarsus as Archbishop of Canterbury, a choice that would prove decisive for the organization and flourishing of the young Church of Anglo-Saxon England.
fontes: Bede the Venerable, «Ecclesiastical History of the English People» IV, 1-2

itens.resumo: A former Benedictine monk, his pontificate unfolded during a period of relative calm in the Monothelite tensions with Constantinople.
itens.corpo: Adeodatus II, a Benedictine monk before his election, governed the Church from 672 to 676, a period of less direct tension with Constantinople compared to that of his closest predecessors, although the Monothelite controversy would only be formally ended a few years later, at the Third Council of Constantinople. He maintained monastic discipline as a reference for the spiritual life of the Roman clergy.

itens.resumo: Roman pope who ended the Schism of Ravenna, dispersed a Nestorian monastic community in Rome, and had the atrium of the old Saint Peter's Basilica paved with marble.
itens.corpo:
Donus (in Latin Donus; died April 11, 678), known as Donus I until 1947, was the son of a Roman named Maurice. He was consecrated Bishop of Rome on November 2, 676, succeeding Adeodatus II after an interval of four months and seventeen days; he was already elderly when elected. Little is known of his life beyond what the Liber Pontificalis records, which attributes to him works of restoration and decoration of Roman churches.

The most significant matter of his pontificate was the reconciliation with Ravenna. In the seventh century, the archbishops of that see had sought for themselves a nearly autocephalous position, apart from Roman authority. Archbishop Maurus had brought this conflict to its height, even exchanging anathemas with Pope Vitalian; his last words to the clergy, according to the chronicler Agnellus, were said to have been "do not submit to the yoke of the Romans." It was his successor, Reparatus, who returned to obedience to the Holy See, ending the schism during the pontificate of Donus. The sources, however, differ on the details: the Liber Pontificalis says that Reparatus was consecrated in Rome, while Agnellus maintains that he was consecrated in Ravenna — a discrepancy for which scholars have still not given an entirely satisfactory explanation.

Another picturesque episode on record is the discovery, in Rome, of a colony of Nestorian monks in the so-called Monasterium Boetianum, a Syrian monastery. Donus is said to have dispersed these monks among various religious houses of the city and handed their monastery over to Roman monks. In relations with Constantinople, his stance was conciliatory: on August 10, 678, Emperor Constantine IV addressed him as "the most holy and blessed archbishop of our ancient Rome and universal pope," seeking to draw him into negotiations with the Patriarch of Constantinople and the Monothelites — negotiations that would lead to the Sixth Ecumenical Council (680-681) and the condemnation of Monothelitism, already under his successor Agatho. The emperor also ordered that the name of Pope Vitalian be restored to the diptychs of the bishops in communion with Constantinople, a measure that brought him difficulties with Patriarch Theodore I.

Donus had the atrium in front of the old Saint Peter's Basilica paved with large blocks of white marble, restored the church of Saint Euphemia on the Appian Way, and repaired the Basilica of Saint Paul Outside the Walls. He governed for only one year, five months, and ten days, dying on April 11, 678 and being buried, on the same day, in Saint Peter's Basilica. His mosaic portrait was once seen in the church of Saint Martina, in the Forum.
fontes: Agnellus of Ravenna, Liber Pontificalis Ecclesiae Ravennatis

itens.resumo: An elderly pope under whose authority the Third Council of Constantinople definitively condemned Monothelitism.
itens.corpo: Agatho, already advanced in age when elected in 678, sent legates to the Third Council of Constantinople (680-681), which would put an end to the Monothelite controversy by solemnly defining that Christ possesses two wills, human and divine, in perfect harmony — ending decades of dispute that had cost Saint Martin I his exile and death. Agatho died a few months before the conclusion of the council. He also resolved a long-standing dispute with the Church of Ravenna, reaffirming that its episcopal consecration depended on Rome.
fontes: Acts of the Third Council of Constantinople (680-681)

itens.resumo: Pope who promulgated in the West the decisions of the Third Council of Constantinople, clarifying that Honorius I had erred through negligence, not through personal heresy.
itens.corpo: Leo II governed for less than a year, between 682 and 683, but it fell to him to formally ratify in the West the decisions of the Third Council of Constantinople against Monothelitism. In commenting on the conciliar condemnation of Honorius I, Leo specified the terms: Honorius did not teach heresy out of personal conviction, but "permitted the immaculate faith to be stained" through negligence in failing to eradicate the error of others with due firmness — a distinction that remains a point of reference in theological debates about this episode.
fontes: Letter of Leo II to Emperor Constantine IV

itens.resumo: Pope who obtained from the Byzantine emperor the waiving of imperial confirmation in papal elections, speeding up succession to the office.
itens.corpo: Benedict II governed between 684 and 685. He obtained from Emperor Constantine IV a concession of great practical reach: from then on, the election of a new pope would no longer have to await confirmation from the distant court of Constantinople, the confirmation of the Byzantine exarch of Ravenna, the imperial representative in Italy, being sufficient — a change that would drastically reduce the length of vacancies between pontificates in the following decades.

itens.resumo: Syrian pope, the first elected under the new rule that dispensed with direct imperial confirmation from Constantinople.
itens.corpo: Of Syrian origin, John V was the first pope elected under the new norm that dispensed with the emperor's direct confirmation in Constantinople, approved shortly before by his predecessor Benedict II. His pontificate, between 685 and 686, was brief, with no major events recorded beyond this procedural change already in force.

itens.resumo: An elderly pope chosen as a consensus candidate between rival factions of the Roman clergy and militia.
itens.corpo: Conon, already of advanced age, was elected in 686 as a compromise candidate between two factions of the Roman clergy and militia who could not agree on other names. His pontificate, brief and without major recorded events, ended with his death the following year, leaving the succession once again disputed between two rival candidates—a deadlock that would be resolved with the election of Sergius I.

itens.resumo: Pope who rejected the canons of the Council in Trullo because they differed from Roman discipline; he introduced the Agnus Dei into the Mass and consolidated Marian feasts.
itens.corpo:
Of Syrian and Sicilian origin, Sergius I governed between 687 and 701. He categorically refused to subscribe to the canons of the so-called Council in Trullo (692), which contained provisions contrary to Western discipline—above all concerning clerical celibacy—and which, in the eyes of Rome, improperly elevated the position of Constantinople; Emperor Justinian II's attempt to arrest him for this refusal was thwarted by the militia of Byzantine Italy, which rose up in defense of the pope.

Sergius introduced into the Roman liturgy the singing of the "Agnus Dei" during the breaking of the bread at Mass, and consolidated in the Roman calendar four great Marian feasts—the Annunciation, the Nativity, the Purification, and the Dormition (Assumption) of Mary—with solemn processions that would become a lasting tradition.
fontes: Acts of the Council in Trullo (692)

itens.resumo: A Greek pope who paid ransom for hostages captured in Lombard raids and faced tensions with the troops of the Byzantine exarch of Ravenna.
itens.corpo: Of Greek origin, John VI governed between 701 and 705. He paid ransoms to free prisoners captured in raids by the Lombard duke Gisulf near Rome, and faced an episode of tension with the exarch of Ravenna, whose troops reportedly tried to arrest him—prevented by Roman militiamen who mobilized in defense of the pope, a sign of the growing popular support for the pontifical office in the face of the distant Byzantine authority.

itens.resumo: A Greek pope, son of a Byzantine official, who avoided direct confrontation when the emperor once again asked him to ratify the canons of the Council in Trullo.
itens.corpo: The son of a high Byzantine official, John VII governed from 705 to 707. He received from Emperor Justinian II a new copy of the canons of the Council in Trullo — the same ones that Sergius I had refused — with a request that he approve at least those he considered acceptable; John chose to return them without a reply, avoiding both ratification and a new open break. He was a notable patron of the arts, commissioning the decoration of several Roman churches with frescoes and mosaics, among them a chapel dedicated to Mary in the old Basilica of Saint Peter.

itens.resumo: A pope whose pontificate lasted little more than three weeks, barely managing to sketch out plans to repair the walls of Rome before he died.
itens.corpo: Sisinnius was elected in January 708, already gravely ill with gout, and governed for little more than three weeks before dying. According to the Liber Pontificalis, he even ordered the preparation of lime to repair the walls of Rome, a work he did not live to see carried out.

itens.resumo: Pope of Syrian origin who traveled in person to Constantinople to negotiate with the emperor — the last visit of a pope to the city before Paul VI, in 1967.
itens.corpo: Of Syrian origin, Constantine reigned from 708 to 715. In 710-711, he traveled in person to Constantinople at the invitation of Emperor Justinian II, to deal with the persistent dispute over the canons of the Council in Trullo — a meeting that resulted in a compromise agreement on the points acceptable to Rome. It was the last time a pope set foot in Constantinople until the visit of Paul VI, in the twentieth century, almost one thousand three hundred years later.

itens.resumo: Pope who opposed the iconoclasm of the Byzantine emperor Leo III and sent Saint Boniface to evangelize the Germanic peoples.
itens.corpo:
Gregory II governed from 715 to 731, in a pontificate of great historical importance on two fronts. Faced with the iconoclast edict promulgated by Emperor Leo III around 726, which ordered the destruction of sacred images, Gregory firmly defended the legitimacy of the veneration of images — a stance that deepened the political distance between Rome and Constantinople, paving the way for the papacy to seek alternative support in the West.

During this same pontificate, Gregory consecrated the Anglo-Saxon monk Boniface as a missionary bishop and sent him to evangelize the still-pagan Germanic peoples beyond the Rhine — a mission that would become one of the most decisive in the history of the Christianization of Europe.
fontes: Correspondence between Gregory II and Saint Boniface

itens.resumo: The last pope to seek Byzantine imperial confirmation; he excommunicated the iconoclasts and appealed to Charles Martel of the Franks against the Lombard threat.
itens.corpo:
Gregory III governed from 731 to 741, being the last pope in history to request Byzantine imperial confirmation of his election, a practice that would fall into disuse after his pontificate, a sign of the growing estrangement between Rome and Constantinople. He convened a Roman synod that excommunicated those who practiced or supported the destruction of sacred images, hardening the position already taken by his predecessor in the iconoclastic controversy.

Faced with renewed Lombard pressure on Roman territories, Gregory III sent appeals for help to Charles Martel, the powerful Frankish ruler who had halted the Muslim advance at the Battle of Poitiers, a first step in the rapprochement between the papacy and the Franks that, decades later, would culminate in the alliance with Charlemagne.
fontes: Letters of Gregory III to Charles Martel

itens.resumo: Pope who legitimized the deposition of the last Merovingian king, opening the way for the rise of Pepin the Short and the Carolingian dynasty.
itens.corpo: Zachary, the last pope of Greek origin for many centuries, governed between 741 and 752, a period in which he personally negotiated with the Lombard king Liutprand the preservation of Roman territories threatened with invasion. His act of greatest historical reach, however, was to answer an inquiry from the Frankish mayor of the palace Pepin the Short: asked whether it was right that he who already held the effective power of the kingdom should truly reign, rather than the merely nominal Merovingian king, Zachary answered that it was—an opinion that Pepin used to depose King Childeric III and be acclaimed king of the Franks in 751, founding the Carolingian dynasty that would change the course of medieval Europe.
itens.imagem_credito: Photo: Sailko — Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0
fontes: Royal Frankish Annals, on Pepin's inquiry

itens.resumo: The pope who crossed the Alps to ask for Frankish protection against the Lombards and received from Pepin the donation of lands that founded the Papal States.
itens.corpo:
Faced with the renewed threat of the Lombard king Aistulf against Rome, Stephen II made an unprecedented decision in 753: he personally crossed the Alps to seek direct help from the Frankish king Pepin the Short, becoming the first pope to visit Frankish lands. In exchange for military support, he solemnly anointed Pepin and his sons as kings of the Franks at Saint-Denis in 754, reinforcing with ecclesiastical blessing the legitimacy of the new Carolingian dynasty.

Pepin, in turn, defeated the Lombards and handed over to Stephen the reconquered lands of the former Byzantine Exarchate of Ravenna — the so-called «Donation of Pepin» of 756 —, an act that created the territorial core of the Papal States, the temporal dominion of the Church that would endure, with changes in extent, until 1870.
fontes: Royal Frankish Annals, on the Donation of Pepin (756)

itens.resumo: Brother and successor of Stephen II, he continued the alliance with the Franks and the organization of the newly formed Papal States.
itens.corpo: Brother of Stephen II, Paul I succeeded him in 757 and maintained the policy of close alliance with the Frankish kings, essential for the security of the territories recently received as a donation from Pepin. He devoted himself to the administrative organization of these domains, still taking shape as a political entity of their own, and to the construction and restoration of Roman churches.

itens.resumo: Pope elected after a violent episode in which a layman usurped the papal throne; he convened a synod that tightened the rules for papal elections.
itens.corpo: The death of Paul I was followed by a tumultuous episode: a lay nobleman, Constantine, was imposed on the papacy by force by his brother, a local duke, and was ordained priest and consecrated bishop in rapid, irregular succession — a usurpation that lasted about a year until it was reversed with violence, including the mutilation of Constantine, a brutal practice common in the power struggles of the time. Elected amid this crisis in 768, Stephen III convened a synod at the Lateran the following year that reaffirmed stricter rules for papal elections, seeking to prevent new lay usurpations.

itens.resumo: A pope allied with Charlemagne, who defeated the Lombard kingdom at his request; under his authority the Second Council of Nicaea restored the veneration of images.
itens.corpo:
One of the longest and most important pontificates of the Carolingian period, that of Adrian I (772-795) consolidated the alliance between the papacy and Charlemagne, son of Pepin: at Adrian's request, as he was threatened by the Lombard king Desiderius, Charlemagne invaded and definitively defeated the Lombard kingdom in 774, confirming and expanding the territorial donation previously made by his father to the Church of Rome.

Under Adrian's authority, the Second Council of Nicaea (787) — the seventh ecumenical council — brought to an end the first phase of Byzantine iconoclasm, solemnly restoring the legitimacy of the veneration of sacred images, a question that had divided the East for decades.
fontes: Acts of the Second Council of Nicaea (787)

itens.resumo: Pope who crowned Charlemagne "Emperor of the Romans" on Christmas Day in the year 800, a milestone in the restoration of the Western Empire.
itens.corpo: Leo III governed from 795 to 816, surviving an attempted assault and mutilation by factions of the Roman nobility in 799, an episode that led him to seek refuge with Charlemagne. On Christmas Day in 800, in Saint Peter's Basilica, he crowned Charlemagne "Emperor of the Romans", an act of enormous symbolic and political weight, which restored, at least nominally, the imperial dignity in the West that had been extinct for more than three centuries, and established a new type of relationship between papal authority and secular power that would mark the whole of the European Middle Ages.
fontes: Royal Frankish Annals, on the coronation of Charlemagne (800)

itens.resumo: Pope who traveled to France to personally crown Louis the Pious, son of Charlemagne, reinforcing the papal role in imperial coronations.
itens.corpo: Stephen IV governed for little more than half a year, between 816 and 817. Following the precedent set by Leo III, he traveled to Reims, in France, to personally crown and anoint Louis the Pious, son and successor of Charlemagne, as emperor — a gesture that reinforced the idea that papal legitimation was a necessary element, and not merely a symbolic one, of Carolingian imperial dignity.
fontes: Royal Frankish Annals, on the coronation of Louis the Pious (816)

itens.resumo: Pope who built notable Roman churches famed for their mosaics, whose pontificate was marked by growing tension with the local nobility.
itens.corpo: Paschal I governed from 817 to 824, devoting himself above all to the construction and restoration of churches in Rome — among them Santa Prassede (Saint Praxedes), whose apse mosaics, including a portrait of the pope himself, are today considered one of the most remarkable ensembles of Byzantine-Roman art of the Carolingian period. His pontificate was marked by growing tension with the Roman nobility; he was even accused — and denied — of involvement in the blinding and murder of two high papal officials, an episode that required an imperial investigation.
fontes: Royal Frankish Annals, on the imperial investigation

itens.resumo: Pope who accepted the «Constitutio Romana», an imperial document that expanded Carolingian oversight over papal elections and governance.
itens.corpo: Elected in 824 under pressure from Emperor Lothair I, Eugene II accepted the so-called «Constitutio Romana», which established closer imperial oversight over the administration of Rome and over the validity of papal elections, reflecting how much Carolingian power had grown over the internal affairs of the papacy since the time of Charlemagne. He also convened a Roman synod devoted to the reform of discipline and the formation of the clergy.

itens.resumo: Bishop of Rome elected in 827, whose pontificate ended a few weeks later with his death.
itens.corpo:
Valentine was born in Rome, in the region of Via Lata, the son of a nobleman named Leontius. According to the Liber Pontificalis, he was taken while still young to the Lateran Palace and ordained a deacon by Pope Paschal I. The same account states that he later served as archdeacon and gained the trust of Paschal I and of his successor, Eugene II.

After the death of Eugene II, the clergy, the nobility, and the people of Rome acclaimed Valentine as Pope. He was taken from the Basilica of Saint Mary Major to the Lateran Palace and enthroned before being ordained a priest, an unusual reversal of the customary order. On the following Sunday, he was consecrated bishop in the Basilica of Saint Peter.

His pontificate took place in 827 and lasted only a few weeks. Historical sources differ as to the exact day of the election, but they record his death on October 10, 827. Valentine died before he could have his election ratified before the Carolingian emperor, and he was succeeded by Gregory IV. His brief pontificate is a sign of the growing participation of the Roman nobility in papal elections in the ninth century.
fontes: Raymond Davis, Lives of the Ninth-Century Popes, Liverpool University Press, 1995
Johann Peter Kirsch, “Pope Valentine”, The Catholic Encyclopedia, 1912 (newadvent.org/cathen/15254b.htm)

itens.resumo: Pope who became directly involved in the succession dispute between Emperor Louis the Pious and his rebellious sons, at a cost to his own moral authority.
itens.corpo: Gregory IV governed between 827 and 844, a period dominated by the succession crisis of the Carolingian Empire. In 833, he sided with the rebellious sons of Emperor Louis the Pious, traveling to the so-called "Field of Lies" (Rotfeld), where Louis's army dissolved without a fight before his sons — an episode that, although it momentarily favored Gregory's position, also exposed the papacy to accusations of excessive political interference in secular dynastic disputes, damaging his prestige among part of the Frankish clergy.
fontes: Annals of the Franks, on the Field of Lies (833)

itens.resumo: Pope during whose pontificate Saracen pirates plundered the Basilicas of Saint Peter and Saint Paul Outside the Walls, which lay outside the walls of Rome.
itens.corpo: Sergius II governed from 844 to 847. In 846, a Saracen (Arab-Muslim) fleet landed near Rome and plundered the Basilicas of Saint Peter and Saint Paul Outside the Walls, both then located outside the fortified perimeter of the city — one of the most traumatic episodes experienced by Rome in the early Middle Ages, which exposed the vulnerability of Saint Peter's Basilica itself to external attacks and would lead his successor to undertake the construction of specific defensive walls to protect the Vatican area.
fontes: Annals of Fulda, on the Saracen sack (846)

itens.resumo: Pope who built the defensive wall around the Vatican after the Saracen sack of 846, and whose fleet defeated the invaders at the Battle of Ostia.
itens.corpo: Leo IV governed between 847 and 855, responding directly to the trauma of the Saracen sack of 846 suffered under his predecessor.
