He organized a naval coalition of Italian maritime cities that defeated a Saracen fleet at the Battle of Ostia (849), and had a fortified wall built around the Vatican Hill and Saint Peter's Basilica — the so-called "Leonine City", which came to physically protect that region of Rome against new attacks.
itens.imagem_credito: Photo: PalauanLibertarian — Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0
fontes: Annals of Fulda, on the Battle of Ostia (849)

itens.resumo: A pope whose election was briefly contested by an antipope; at this point, late chronicles inserted the legend, with no historical basis, of the "Popess Joan".
itens.corpo:
Benedict III was elected in 855, but his accession was contested for a few months by Anastasius the Librarian, a cleric supported by factions linked to the imperial court, who proclaimed himself pope before being removed. Benedict III took up the government effectively shortly afterward.

It is precisely at this point in the succession — between Leo IV and Benedict III — that chronicles written centuries later, beginning in the thirteenth century, inserted the legend of a supposed "Popess Joan", a woman who allegedly occupied the papal throne disguised as a man. There is no source contemporary with the events, nor from the immediately following centuries, that mentions such a figure — modern historical research considers the account a late fabrication, probably satirical or polemical in character, without any documentary basis. This collection does not include her in the numbering of pontiffs because it is not a historically supported case.

itens.resumo: Ninth-century pope who asserted papal authority before bishops and the emperor, and intervened in the schism with Photius of Constantinople.
itens.corpo: Bishop of Rome from 858 to 867, Nicholas I is considered by many historians one of the most assertive popes of the High Middle Ages in affirming Petrine authority, intervening in the matrimonial disputes of Frankish kings and deposing bishops whom he judged to have acted unjustly. His pontificate coincided with the beginning of the so-called Photian Schism, a dispute over the legitimacy of the patriarchate of Constantinople that foreshadowed tensions that would culminate, two centuries later, in the East-West Schism of 1054.

itens.resumo: Pope who approved the liturgical use of the Slavic language in the evangelizing mission of Cyril and Methodius among the Slavic peoples.
itens.corpo: Adrian II governed from 867 to 872, in a pontificate marked by personal tragedy: his wife and daughter, from before his ordination (he was a widower when elected), were kidnapped and murdered in an episode of Roman political violence. On the ecclesiastical front, he approved the request of the missionaries Cyril and Methodius to celebrate the liturgy in Old Church Slavonic among the peoples of Moravia, a decision of great consequence for the formation of Slavic Christian identity, and he continued the efforts to end the Photian Schism with Constantinople.
fontes: Acts on the mission of Cyril and Methodius

itens.resumo: An energetic pope who faced Saracen incursions into Italy and the Photian Schism; the first pontiff known with certainty to have been assassinated in a conspiracy.
itens.corpo:
John VIII governed between 872 and 882 with an energy unusual for the period, crowning Charles the Bald as emperor and confronting at close range the Saracen threat to the Italian coast — at one point he even paid tribute to contain immediate attacks, while at the same time seeking to form military alliances against the invaders. He also worked to bring the Photian Schism with Constantinople definitively to an end.

His end was violent: according to accounts from the time, he was first poisoned by members of his own circle and, since the poison acted too slowly for the conspirators, was finally killed by blows — making him the first pope documented with certainty as the victim of an assassination by internal conspiracy.
fontes: Annals of Fulda, on his death

itens.resumo: A pope whose election, while he was already bishop of another see, is one of the first cases of "episcopal translation" to the papacy; he restored the future Pope Formosus to communion.
itens.corpo: Marinus I, bishop of Cerveteri before being elected pope in 882, had his election questioned by later jurists for violating the norm then being consolidated that a bishop should not be transferred from one see to another — a precedent that, decades later, would fuel controversies over the validity of ordinations of the period. He restored to ecclesiastical communion Bishop Formosus, who had been excommunicated during the previous pontificate for political reasons, a decision that Formosus himself would recall when he was elected pope some years later.

itens.resumo: Pope with a brief pontificate, who died while traveling to a synod convened by Emperor Charles the Fat.
itens.corpo: Adrian III governed for little more than a year, between 884 and 885, dying on the way to an imperial assembly convened by Charles the Fat in Germany. Few concrete details of his government have survived in the sources of the period; he has been venerated as a saint since the Middle Ages, although his formal canonization was only officially confirmed in 1891.

itens.resumo: Pope who governed an impoverished and threatened Rome, having to appeal to the Frankish rulers for military protection.
itens.corpo: Stephen V governed from 885 to 891, a period of scarce resources and of lacking effective military protection for Rome, which led him to appeal repeatedly to the Carolingian rulers for help against external threats. He also had to deal with the tensions left by the Slavic mission of Cyril and Methodius after the latter's death, in the face of pressure from the German-speaking clergy opposed to the liturgical use of Slavonic.

itens.resumo: Pope whose corpse was exhumed and put on trial by his successor Stephen VI, in one of the darkest episodes in papal history — the so-called "Cadaver Synod."
itens.corpo:
Formosus, Bishop of Porto before being elected pope in 891 — another "episcopal translation" that would generate a posthumous legal dispute —, governed during a period of intense political instability in Italy, crowning different rival claimants to the imperial throne as alliances shifted, which earned him lasting enmity among influential Roman factions.

He died in 896. Less than a year later, his successor Stephen VI, under pressure from factions hostile to Formosus, ordered the exhumation of his body, which was dressed in papal vestments, seated on a throne, and formally tried in a synod — an episode known as the "Cadaver Synod" (Synodus Horrenda). Found guilty, the body was mutilated and thrown into the Tiber River. Later popes would reverse this judgment and restore the memory of Formosus, in one of the most bizarre and sinister chapters in the entire history of the papacy.
fontes: Acts of the Cadaver Synod (897, under Stephen VI)

itens.resumo: Pope of a very brief pontificate, elected despite having already been removed from the clergy twice before for misconduct.
itens.corpo: Boniface VI was elected in 896 despite having already been stripped of his clerical status on two earlier occasions for immoral conduct — an eligibility that would technically have required a special dispensation, which is not clearly documented. He governed for only fifteen days before dying, according to the accounts of the time, of complications from gout.

itens.resumo: Pope responsible for the "Cadaver Synod," the posthumous trial of the exhumed body of Formosus; he himself would be deposed and strangled in prison shortly afterward.
itens.corpo:
In 897, Stephen VI ordered the exhumation of the body of his predecessor Formosus—who had died a year earlier—in order to subject him to a formal trial for alleged canonical irregularities in his election and in ordinations he had performed. The corpse, dressed in papal vestments and seated on a throne for the trial, was declared guilty, had the fingers used for blessing mutilated, and was thrown into the Tiber River.

The episode shocked even contemporaries who were hardly sensitive to the political violence of the period, and it turned against Stephen VI himself: months later, a popular uprising deposed him, imprisoned him, and strangled him while still in prison—an end as violent as the trial he had ordered.

itens.resumo: Pope of a brief pontificate who began to reverse the acts of the "Cadaver Synod" against the memory of Formosus.
itens.corpo: Elected right after the fall of Stephen VI, Romanus governed for about four months in 897, beginning the process of reversing the judgments made against the memory of Formosus at the "Cadaver Synod" — a process that his immediate successors would complete. He himself was removed from office shortly afterward and sent to a monastery.

itens.resumo: A pope who, in a pontificate of little more than twenty days, formally annulled the "Cadaver Synod" and gave Formosus a dignified burial.
itens.corpo: In a pontificate of only twenty days, at the end of 897, Theodore II completed the rehabilitation of Formosus's memory: he formally annulled the decisions of the "Cadaver Synod," recovered the remains thrown into the Tiber, and ordered that they be buried again with the honors due to a pope, completely reversing the episode promoted by Stephen VI months earlier.

itens.resumo: Pope who definitively confirmed the rehabilitation of Formosus and, by synod, forbade that a dead pope ever be put on trial again.
itens.corpo: John IX governed between 898 and 900, confirming in synod the full rehabilitation of the memory of Formosus already begun by his immediate predecessors, and expressly ordering that no pope's corpse could ever again be subjected to trial — a norm that directly answered the recent trauma of the "Cadaver Synod." He also sought to restore discipline and order to the process of papal election, shaken by the tumultuous succession of the preceding years.

itens.resumo: Pope who faced the Magyar invasions of northern Italy and crowned Louis of Provence as emperor.
itens.corpo: Benedict IV governed from 900 to 903, a period in which the Magyars (Hungarians) intensified their devastating incursions into northern Italy, a threat added to the already familiar Saracen pressure on the coast. He crowned Louis the Blind of Provence as emperor, in a context of political fragmentation of the former Carolingian realm.

itens.resumo: A pope deposed and imprisoned just weeks after his election by a rival usurper; he died in prison, probably murdered.
itens.corpo: Leo V was elected in July 903, but he governed for only about a month before being deposed and imprisoned by the priest Christopher, who proclaimed himself pope in his place — yet another episode of the chronic instability that marked the Roman papacy at this turn from the ninth to the tenth century. Leo V died in prison, probably murdered on the orders of his usurper, whom the Church today does not recognize as a legitimate pope.

itens.resumo: Pope who regained the throne by deposing a rival, marking the beginning of the period in which the powerful Roman Theophylact family came to control the papacy.
itens.corpo: Sergius III had been a defeated candidate in a papal election years earlier; he regained power in 904 with military support, ending the brief pontificate of the antipope Christopher, whom he had imprisoned. His pontificate marks the beginning of the period that historians call the «saeculum obscurum» («dark age»), in which the influential Roman Theophylact family — above all through Theodora and her daughter Marozia — came to control the choice of popes in practice for decades. Contemporary sources, hostile to him, claim that Sergius had a son with Marozia, who decades later would become pope as John XI.

itens.resumo: Pope with a brief pontificate, already under the dominant influence of the Theophylact family over the government of Rome.
itens.corpo: Anastasius III governed between 911 and 913, in a period when the Theophylact family already exercised effective control over the affairs of Rome, leaving the pope little room for independent action. The sources of the period record few acts of government of his own during his short pontificate.

itens.resumo: Bishop of Rome during a brief pontificate between 913 and 914, in a period of strong aristocratic influence over the papacy.
itens.corpo:
Lando, also called Landus or Landone, was elected Bishop of Rome between August and September 913, although the sources differ on the exact beginning of his pontificate. He was a native of the Sabina and, according to the Liber Pontificalis, the son of a Lombard count named Taino, connected with Fornovo.

His government took place during the so-called saeculum obscurum, when aristocratic families exercised great influence over Roman politics. The length of the pontificate also appears differently in the sources: the Liber Pontificalis gives four months and twenty-two days, while a tradition linked to the Abbey of Farfa and the chronicler Flodoard point to a period of close to six months. For this reason, the dates should be treated as approximate.

The only known act of his government was a donation to the diocese of Sabina, used to restore the cathedral of Saint Saviour after a raid by Arab plunderers. No document from Lando's chancery has survived. His pontificate ended between February and the end of March 914, when John X was elected. Lando remains the only Pope to have used this name.
fontes: Umberto Longo, “Landone, papa”, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, vol. 63, 2004
Flodoard of Reims, historical reference cited in studies of the pontificate

itens.resumo: Pope who personally led a victorious military coalition against a Saracen base in Italy; he would later die in prison, probably smothered on the orders of Marozia.
itens.corpo:
John X governed between 914 and 928, in a pontificate marked by unusual vigor: he organized and personally led, at the head of troops, a coalition of Italian and Byzantine forces that in 915 destroyed a fortified Saracen base on the Garigliano River, a threat that had tormented central Italy for decades — one of the rare medieval popes to directly command a victorious military campaign.

Over time, he became a rival of the increasingly powerful Marozia, who had already dominated Roman politics for years. Around 928, he was imprisoned on her orders and died in prison shortly afterward, most likely smothered — yet another victim of the political violence of the «saeculum obscurum».

itens.resumo: Bishop of Rome with a brief pontificate, exercised during the Roman political crisis of the tenth century.
itens.corpo:
Leo VI was a Roman and the son of Christopher, who had held the office of primicerius under Pope John VIII. Before his election, he was cardinal-priest of Santa Susanna. The ancient sources and historical studies do not allow the day of his election to be fixed with certainty; the historiographical tradition places it in the first half or the middle of 928, during the period known as the saeculum obscurum.

His pontificate lasted about seven months. Leo confirmed decisions concerning the ecclesiastical situation of Dalmatia, continuing investigations begun by John X, and granted the pallium to Archbishop John of Salona. He also appealed for the defense of Rome against Arab incursions. The surviving documentation about his governance is scarce, and does not allow a broad pontifical program to be attributed to him.

The date of his death also appears with variations in the sources: the Catholic Encyclopedia considers February 929 probable, if the election took place in June 928, while other compilations record February 12, 929. For this reason, the archive keeps the approximate interval "c. June 928 – February 929". Tradition holds that he was buried in Saint Peter's Basilica. Leo VI is counted as the 123rd Pope in the historical lists that do not include antipopes.
fontes: Horace Mann, "Pope Leo VI", The Catholic Encyclopedia, 1910 (newadvent.org/cathen/09159c.htm)
Liber Pontificalis, ed. Louis Duchesne, vol. II, p. 242
Flodoard of Reims, reference cited in the historical documentation of the pontificate

itens.resumo: A Roman cardinal raised to the papacy by Marozia of Tusculum as a transitional solution, until her own son could take over the see.
itens.corpo:
Stephen VII (in Latin Stephanus VII; Rome, c. 880 — Rome, March 15, 931), born to a father named Teudemund, was cardinal-priest of the basilica of Saint Anastasia before being raised to the See of Peter. He was elected around February 3, 929, succeeding Leo VI, in a period when the effective government of Rome was in the hands of the noblewoman Marozia, daughter of the senator Theophylact I and of Theodora. Historiography usually describes this interval as the saeculum obscurum or "pornocracy," because of the dominance that the women of the Theophylact family exercised over Roman politics and over the choice of pontiffs.

Stephen's election was conducted under the direct influence of Marozia, who was then consolidating her power: the widow of Alberic I of Spoleto and later of Guy of Tuscany, she would still marry, in 932, Hugh of Arles, King of Italy. Several scholars maintain that Stephen was chosen as a transitional pope, a provisional solution meant to fill the see until John, Marozia's son, reached the age to assume the papacy. Indeed, upon Stephen's death he was succeeded, in 931, by John XI himself, Marozia's son — according to the tradition recorded in the Liber Pontificalis and in the Antapodosis of Liutprand of Cremona, born of her relationship with Pope Sergius III.

Little is known of his acts. The Liber Pontificalis and later documentation attribute to him the granting of privileges to monasteries, among them that of Saint Vincent at Volturno and two convents in Gaul. There is also a record that, upon freeing himself from the oppression of Hugh of Arles, Stephen granted Cante di Gabrielli the office of papal governor of Gubbio and control of several fortresses in the region.

The validity of his pontificate is a matter of debate, since, like his predecessor Leo VI, he was elected while Pope John X was still imprisoned — if the deposition of John X is considered invalid, so too would be the pontificates of Leo VI and Stephen. The date of his death, around March 15, 931, is accepted by most sources; it has been speculated that he was assassinated, but the hypothesis is not unanimous. He was buried in Saint Peter's Basilica. His numbering is problematic: because of the pope-elect Stephen, who died before consecration in 752, the present pontiff was called Stephen VIII by sources prior to the 1960s, the period in which the modern numbering (Stephen VII) became established.

itens.resumo: A young man raised to the papacy by his mother Marozia, then the most powerful woman in Rome; he was made a political hostage by his own half-brother when she lost power.
itens.corpo: John XI, still a young man, was placed on the papal throne in 931 by his mother Marozia, who by then had dominated Rome for more than a decade — hostile sources of the time even name him as the son of Pope Sergius III, although historians dispute his paternity. In 932, John's half-brother, Alberic II, led an uprising that removed Marozia from secular power over Rome; John XI, kept on as pope, was practically confined to the Lateran Palace, without real political power, under the new guardianship of Alberic, who would go on to control Rome for the following decades.

itens.resumo: Pope who reigned under the political control of Alberic II and supported the monastic reform of Cluny.
itens.corpo: Leo VII governed between 936 and 939, already under the stable political control exercised by Alberic II over Rome. He was distinguished by his support for the monastic reform then underway from the abbey of Cluny, in Burgundy, a movement that sought to restore the rigor of Benedictine observance in lax monasteries — a rare sign of spiritual vitality amid the political turbulence of the period.

itens.resumo: A pope who governed under the rule of Alberic II and suffered an attack by Roman opponents that left him disfigured.
itens.corpo: Stephen VIII governed between 939 and 942, under the consolidated political control of Alberic II. According to accounts from the period, he was the victim of an attack by opposing Roman factions that left him physically disfigured, an episode that illustrates the violence still present in the struggle for power in Rome even under Alberic's relatively stable rule.

itens.resumo: Pope who, under the rule of Alberic II, continued to support the Benedictine monastic reform under way at the time.
itens.corpo: Marinus II reigned from 942 to 946, a period of relative stability under Alberic II's firm secular control over Rome. He continued the papal support for the Benedictine monastic reform that was gaining strength from Cluny, and also restored some Roman churches.

itens.resumo: Pope who reigned during the last years of Alberic II's rule over Rome, a period in which the influence of the Germanic king Otto I over Italy was beginning to grow.
itens.corpo: Agapetus II governed from 946 to 955, still under the political tutelage of Alberic II, who, before dying in 954, obtained from the Roman nobles an oath that his son Octavian would be the next pope — a dynastic arrangement that would be fulfilled with the election of the future John XII. During this pontificate, the influence of the Germanic king Otto I over Italian affairs was beginning to grow, foreshadowing the decisive intervention he would exercise in the following decade.

itens.resumo: A pope still in his adolescence who crowned Otto I as emperor in 962 — restoring the imperial title in the West — but later conspired against him and was deposed.
itens.corpo:
Son of Alberic II, Octavian took the papacy with the name John XII while still an adolescent, at around eighteen years of age, temporarily uniting in the same person the secular government of Rome inherited from his father and the papal dignity. Sources from the period, above all the chronicler Liutprand of Cremona — a hostile but contemporary witness — describe a personal conduct marked by scandals, although his account must be read with due critical caution regarding polemical exaggerations.

In 962, John XII crowned the German king Otto I as emperor — an act of enormous historical weight, which formally restored the imperial dignity in the West after decades of effective vacancy, giving rise to what would become the Holy Roman Empire. Months later, fearing the growth of Otto's power, John XII conspired against him; once discovered, he was deposed by a Roman synod convened under imperial pressure in 963, which elected Leo VIII in his place. John would briefly regain power after Otto's departure from Italy, dying shortly afterward.

itens.resumo: Pope elected by the Romans in defiance of the will of Emperor Otto I, who was already supporting Leo VIII; he was later deposed and exiled.
itens.corpo: After the death of John XII, the Romans elected Benedict V in 964, in direct defiance of the will of Emperor Otto I, who had already imposed Leo VIII as pope the previous year. Otto besieged Rome, forced the city to submit, and Benedict V was formally deposed at a synod presided over by Leo VIII himself, and was then exiled to Hamburg, in northern Germany, where he would die a few years later. The relative legitimacy of Benedict V and Leo VIII in this confusing episode is still debated today by historians of the papacy.

itens.resumo: Pope installed by Otto I after the deposition of John XII, whose legitimacy was contested by part of the Romans even during his own pontificate.
itens.corpo: Leo VIII was elevated to the papacy in 963 by a Roman synod convened under strong pressure from Emperor Otto I, who sought to replace John XII — still formally pope and alive at that moment, which made the legitimacy of Leo's elevation contested by part of the Roman clergy and nobility from the outset. He needed Otto's direct military support to maintain his position and, later, to depose the rival Benedict V, elected by the Romans after the death of John XII.

itens.resumo: Pope restored with the military support of Otto I after being exiled by the Roman nobility; he presided over the marriage that united the empires of the West and of Byzantium.
itens.corpo: John XIII governed from 965 to 972, but early in his pontificate he was kidnapped and exiled by factions of the Roman nobility unhappy with his close ties to Emperor Otto I — he was only able to retake the throne months later, with direct imperial military support. Under his authority, the marriage between the future Emperor Otto II and the Byzantine princess Theophano was celebrated in 972, a union that sought to seal the reconciliation, albeit a temporary one, between the Western Empire restored by Otto I and the Byzantine Empire of the East.
fontes: Records of the marriage of Otto II and Theophano (972)

itens.resumo: Pope imprisoned and strangled by a rival Roman faction after the death of Emperor Otto I, who had supported him.
itens.corpo: Benedict VI, elected in 973 with the support of Emperor Otto I, lost his protection when the emperor died a few months later. A Roman faction led by the Crescentii family took advantage of the power vacuum to depose him, imprison him and, according to the accounts of the period, strangle him in 974, installing an antipope in his place — an episode that reopened the cycle of political violence that had marked the «saeculum obscurum» decades earlier.

itens.resumo: Pope who restored order in Rome after the murder of Benedict VI, with the support of the new emperor Otto II.
itens.corpo: Benedict VII was elevated to the papacy in 974 with the support of Emperor Otto II, restoring some stability after the murder of Benedict VI and the deposition of the antipope who had succeeded him. He continued papal support for the Benedictine monastic reform under way since Cluny, and reigned for nearly a decade without the violent upheavals of the recent past.

itens.resumo: Pope appointed by Otto II shortly before the emperor's death; without imperial protection, he was imprisoned by the rival antipope who had returned, and died in prison.
itens.corpo: John XIV was nominated to the papacy by Emperor Otto II in 983, but the emperor died a few months later, leaving the new pope without political support. The antipope Boniface VII, who had fled Rome years earlier after an episode of usurpation, returned to the city and managed to imprison John XIV, who died in prison in 984, probably of starvation — one more episode of the violent instability that repeatedly marked the Roman papacy in this period.

itens.resumo: The pope who carried out the first formal canonization of a saint through a documented pontifical process: Saint Ulrich of Augsburg, in 993.
itens.corpo: John XV governed between 985 and 996, a period in which the powerful Roman Crescentii family exercised political control equivalent to that which the Theophylacti had exercised decades earlier. His pontificate is remembered for an important procedural milestone: in 993, he formally canonized Saint Ulrich of Augsburg at a Roman synod, this being the first well-documented case of a canonization carried out directly by papal decision, foreshadowing the centralized process that the Church would fully develop in the following centuries.
fontes: Acts of the Roman Synod on the Canonization of Saint Ulrich (993)

itens.resumo: The first pope of Germanic origin, appointed at the urging of his cousin, Emperor Otto III; he was driven out of Rome by a coup and later restored by force.
itens.corpo: Bruno of Carinthia, cousin of Emperor Otto III, became in 996 the first pope of Germanic origin in history, taking the name Gregory V. Shortly afterward, a revolt led by Crescentius II drove him out of Rome and installed an antipope in his place. Otto III returned to Italy with an army, restored Gregory V to the throne, had Crescentius II executed, and severely punished the deposed antipope — an episode that demonstrated, once again, how much the papacy depended on imperial military support to maintain itself in the face of the Roman factions.

itens.resumo: The first French pope and one of the greatest scholars of his time in mathematics; late legends, with no historical basis, accused him of sorcery because of this learning.
itens.corpo:
Gerbert of Aurillac, tutor to the young Emperor Otto III, became in 999 the first pope of French origin, taking the name Sylvester II. Before his election, he was already recognized as one of the greatest scholars of his time, with contributions to mathematics, to the construction of astronomical instruments, and to the spread, in the Latin West, of the improved abacus and of numerals of Arabic origin.

This same knowledge, unusual for the era, fueled legends centuries later, with no historical basis whatsoever, that accused him of having obtained knowledge through pacts with occult forces — late fabrications that modern historical research completely rejects, recognizing in him one of the greatest intellectuals of his century.

itens.resumo: A Roman named Giovanni Sicco, chosen by John Crescentius, who governed the Church for about seven months in 1003, between the shadow of the Crescentii family and the evangelizing mission of Bruno of Querfurt.
itens.corpo:
John XVII (in Latin Ioannes XVII; died November 6, 1003), born Giovanni Sicco, was bishop of Rome and nominal ruler of the Papal States for about seven months in 1003. He was the son of another Giovanni Sicco and was born in the region of Rome then called Biveretica. Before entering the priesthood, he had been married and had three sons who also embraced the ecclesiastical life: John, bishop of Praeneste; Peter, deacon; and Andrew, secundicerius. In 1040, the three sons erected an epitaph in Santa Prassede, declaring themselves to be of the family of Pope Sicco.

He was elected on May 16, 1003, succeeding Sylvester II. His election was the work of John Crescentius, a Roman nobleman who held the effective power in the city in opposition to Emperor Otto III. Crescentius sought docile candidates, whose loyalty to the ruling family would weigh more than any ambition of their own, and John XVII was one of the pontiffs "chosen and eclipsed" by the patrician. His brief reign, however, was not entirely inert: he approved the mission led by Bruno of Querfurt in Eastern Europe, and Bruno even asked him for authorization for his companion Benedict to evangelize among the Slavs.

He died on November 6, 1003 (some texts propose the 9th, without consensus) and was buried in the Lateran Basilica, between the two doors of the main façade. According to John the Deacon, his epitaph began by stating: "here is the tomb of the supreme John, who is said to be pope, for so he was called". His successor, John XVIII, was also appointed by Crescentius.

His numbering reflects the medieval confusions in the sequence of the popes named John. He took the number XVII because of the antipope John XVI, and some historians "corrected" his number to XVIII by assuming the existence of a John XIV bis who never actually existed; for this reason he is sometimes written John XVII (XVIII). The error in the textual transmission of the entry on John XIV in the Liber Pontificalis is the root of these discrepancies, which reached only XXIII even though there have been only twenty-one legitimate popes of that name.

itens.resumo: A pope who, in a gesture rare for the time, resigned his office and withdrew to monastic life before he died.
itens.corpo: John XVIII governed between 1003 and 1009, still under considerable influence from the Crescentii family over Roman affairs. At the end of his pontificate, he voluntarily resigned the papacy — a rare gesture in medieval history — and withdrew to live as a monk in a Roman monastery, where he spent his last days.

itens.resumo: Pope whose pontificate is poorly documented, reigning in the waning days of the Crescentii family's political influence over Rome.
itens.corpo: Sergius IV governed between 1009 and 1012, in the last years in which the Crescentii family still held some influence over Roman politics, about to be replaced by the dominance of the Counts of Tusculum, who would dominate the papacy for the following decades. Little is known in detail about concrete acts of his government.

itens.resumo: Pope from the family of the Counts of Tusculum who crowned Emperor Henry II and introduced the "Filioque" into the Creed sung in Rome, at the emperor's request.
itens.corpo:
A member of the influential family of the Counts of Tusculum, who would replace the Crescentii in dominating Roman politics, Benedict VIII governed between 1012 and 1024. He crowned the Germanic king Henry II as emperor in 1014, and organized naval resistance against Saracen incursions that threatened Sardinia and the Italian coast.

It was also at the request of Henry II that Benedict VIII introduced, in 1014, the clause "Filioque" ("and from the Son") into the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed sung in the Roman liturgy — a practice that had already been common for centuries in Spain and in the Frankish kingdoms, but until then absent from the liturgy of Rome itself. The Roman adoption of this formula, concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son, would become one of the most persistent points of theological friction with the Churches of the East.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, no. 246 (on the Filioque)

itens.resumo: Brother of Benedict VIII, he was ordained and consecrated in rapid, irregular succession on the same day as his election; he crowned Emperor Conrad II.
itens.corpo: Brother of Benedict VIII, John XIX was still a layman when he was elected pope in 1024, and was ordained to all the orders of the clergy and consecrated bishop of Rome on the same day — an exceptionally rapid succession, made possible by the influence of the family of the Counts of Tusculum, who thus kept control of the See of Rome. He crowned the German king Conrad II as emperor in 1027.

itens.resumo: The only pope in history to hold the office three times; he sold the papacy to his own godfather in 1045, one of the most notorious cases of simony ever recorded.
itens.corpo:
A nephew of the two previous popes, Benedict IX came to the papacy at a very young age, in 1032, thanks to the continued influence of the family of the Counts of Tusculum — his exact age at the election is debated by the sources, but it was certainly unusual for the office. His personal conduct, according to hostile accounts from his own time and from later generations, was scandalous even by the already low standards of the period.

In 1045, under pressure from rival Roman factions, Benedict IX literally sold the papacy to his own godfather, the archpriest John Gratian, who took office as Gregory VI — one of the most notorious and best documented cases of simony (the sale of ecclesiastical office) in the entire history of the Church. Even so, Benedict IX would return to power twice more in the following years, amid the succession chaos that would lead to the decisive intervention of Emperor Henry III at the Synod of Sutri (1046), and was definitively removed after the third attempt, in 1048.
fontes: Acts of the Synod of Sutri (1046)

itens.resumo: A pope briefly installed by a rival Roman faction while Benedict IX still claimed the office, in one of the most confusing episodes of medieval papal succession.
itens.corpo: Sylvester III was elevated to the papacy in early 1045 by a Roman faction opposed to the family of the Counts of Tusculum, while Benedict IX — away from Rome at that moment, but still claiming legitimacy — technically remained pope in the eyes of another part of the clergy. Sylvester was expelled from Rome by supporters of Benedict IX a few weeks later, and his position in this confusing episode continues to be debated among historians of the papacy to this day.

itens.resumo: An archpriest who bought the papacy from his own godson Benedict IX, apparently with the intention of ending the scandal; he was deposed for simony at the Synod of Sutri.
itens.corpo:
John Gratian, an archpriest respected for his personal reputation, paid a sum to his godson Benedict IX in 1045 so that the latter would resign the papacy, taking office as Gregory VI — a transaction that, according to some accounts, was intended to end the scandal of the previous pontificate, but which nonetheless constituted simony, the buying or selling of an ecclesiastical office, one of the gravest offenses recognized by canon law.

Emperor Henry III, alarmed by the three-way succession deadlock between Benedict IX, Sylvester III and Gregory VI, convened the Synod of Sutri in 1046, which deposed all three — Gregory VI by acknowledging the irregularity of his own elevation — and opened the way for a series of reforming popes appointed under German influence, the starting point of what would become the great Gregorian Reform of the late eleventh century.
fontes: Acts of the Synod of Sutri (1046)

itens.resumo: German bishop raised to the papacy by Emperor Henry III after the Synod of Sutri, beginning the series of reforming popes who preceded the Gregorian Reform.
itens.corpo: Bishop of Bamberg, in Germany, Clement II was appointed by Henry III right after the Synod of Sutri deposed the three rival claimants to the papacy; he was consecrated and crowned Henry III himself as emperor on the same day, in December 1046. He began concrete efforts to combat simony, starting a succession of popes of German origin, appointed through imperial influence but genuinely committed to the reform of ecclesiastical discipline — direct forerunners of the Gregorian Reform that would mark the second half of the 11th century. He died less than a year later, in circumstances that modern examinations of his remains linked to lead poisoning, possibly of medicinal and accidental origin.
fontes: Acts of the Synod of Sutri (1046)
Forensic study on the remains of Clement II (2007)

itens.resumo: Pope of the eleventh century, central figure of the Investiture Controversy and of the episode of Canossa with Emperor Henry IV.
itens.corpo: Hildebrand of Sovana, elected pope in 1073, is the central figure of the Gregorian Reform: an effort to free the appointment of bishops and abbots from the interference of kings and emperors ("lay investiture") and to reaffirm ecclesiastical discipline, including clerical celibacy. The conflict with Emperor Henry IV led to his excommunication in 1076 and to the famous episode of Canossa in January 1077, when the emperor presented himself as a penitent before the pope. The underlying dispute would only be resolved decades later, with the Concordat of Worms (1122). Gregory VII died in exile, in Salerno.

itens.resumo: Eleventh-century pope who, at the Council of Clermont, called the First Crusade to come to the aid of the Christians of the East.
itens.corpo: Elected in 1088, Urban II is remembered above all for the speech he delivered at Clermont, in France, in November 1095, calling Christian knights to come to the aid of the Byzantine Empire and to free Jerusalem from Muslim rule, thus giving rise to the First Crusade. He continued the Gregorian Reform and did not live to learn of the capture of Jerusalem in 1099, which occurred a few days after his death. He was beatified in 1881.

itens.resumo: Pope of the early thirteenth century, under whose pontificate medieval papal authority reached its highest point; he convened the Fourth Lateran Council.
itens.corpo: Elected in 1198 at the age of 37, Lotario dei Conti di Segni exercised a decisive influence on the European politics of his time, arbitrating succession disputes between kings and imposing interdicts on entire kingdoms. He informally approved the new mendicant orders of Francis of Assisi and (later formalized) of Dominic of Guzmán. He convened the Fourth Lateran Council (1215), one of the most important of the Middle Ages, which established the obligation of annual confession and Paschal communion and fixed the term "transubstantiation" for the Eucharistic doctrine.

itens.resumo: Thirteenth-century pope who promulgated the Decretals, a compilation of canon law, and canonized Francis of Assisi and Dominic de Guzmán.
itens.corpo: A nephew of Innocent III, Ugolino di Segni was elected pope in 1227, already in his eighties, and had a long and combative pontificate, marked by recurring conflicts with Emperor Frederick II. He commissioned Raymond of Peñafort to compile the «Decretals of Gregory IX» (1234), which systematically organized medieval canon law and remained in force, in part, until the 1917 Code. He personally canonized Francis of Assisi (1228), Anthony of Lisbon (1232) and Dominic de Guzmán (1234), personal friends whom he had known during their lifetimes.

itens.resumo: Pope of the late thirteenth century whose conflict with King Philip IV of France marked the end of the papacy's medieval hegemony over the European kingdoms.
itens.corpo: Elected in 1294, Boniface VIII instituted the first Jubilee in the history of the Church, in 1300, drawing crowds of pilgrims to Rome. His pontificate is remembered above all for the conflict with King Philip IV of France over the taxation of the clergy and the limits of royal authority, which led him to publish the bull «Unam Sanctam» (1302), an extreme affirmation of the supremacy of spiritual power over temporal power. The conflict culminated in the outrage of Anagni (1303), when agents of the French king held him prisoner for days; he died a few weeks later. The episode marked the beginning of the decline of medieval papal power over the European kingdoms.

itens.resumo: French pope of the early fourteenth century who moved the papal seat to Avignon, beginning the period known as the Avignon Captivity.
itens.corpo: Elected in 1305, the Frenchman Bertrand de Got never came to reside in Rome; in 1309 he established the papal Curia in Avignon, in southern France, under heavy influence from the French crown — a period that would last almost seventy years and that historical tradition dubbed the «Avignon Captivity», in allusion to the biblical exile in Babylon. Under pressure from King Philip IV, he suppressed the Order of the Templars in 1312, at the Council of Vienne.

itens.resumo: Fourteenth-century pope who, partly heeding the appeals of Saint Catherine of Siena, ended the Avignon Captivity and returned to Rome in 1377.
itens.corpo: The last of the Avignon popes, Gregory XI faced insistent appeals — among them those of Saint Catherine of Siena, who traveled in person to Avignon to persuade him — for the papal seat to return to Rome. In 1377 he carried out the return, ending almost seventy years of French residence of the Curia. His death the following year would be followed by a contested papal election that would trigger the Western Schism (1378-1417), with rival popes and antipopes.
itens.imagem_credito: Photo: Henri Auguste César Serrur — Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0

itens.resumo: Pope whose election at the Council of Constance in 1417 ended the Western Schism between rival popes and antipopes.
itens.corpo: Oddone Colonna was elected pope by the Council of Constance in November 1417, ending almost forty years of division in which as many as three claimants to the papal throne coexisted — in Rome, Avignon and Pisa. His election, accepted by all of Latin Christendom, restored the institutional unity of the Western Church. In the following years he reorganized the papal administration and physically restored Rome, which the Curia's absence had left impoverished.

itens.resumo: Humanist pope of the mid-fifteenth century, founder of the Vatican Apostolic Library.
itens.corpo: Elected in 1447, Tommaso Parentucelli is considered the first pope of Renaissance humanism, having gathered a vast collection of Greek and Latin manuscripts that would become the core of the Vatican Apostolic Library, formally founded during his pontificate. He promoted the urban reconstruction of Rome and received the news, in 1453, of the fall of Constantinople to the Ottoman Turks, an event that deeply shook European Christendom.

itens.resumo: Spanish pope of the late fifteenth century, under whose pontificate the Treaty of Tordesillas was concluded, dividing the lands yet to be discovered between Portugal and Spain.
itens.corpo: Rodrigo Borgia, elected pope in 1492, is one of the most controversial figures in papal history, remembered both for his political and diplomatic activity and for a family life incompatible with the standards now expected of the office. In 1493 he issued the bulls that laid the foundation for the Treaty of Tordesillas (1494), dividing the newly discovered lands outside Europe between the crowns of Portugal and Castile — a decision with direct consequences for the colonization and evangelization of the Americas. The collection records the historical fact without endorsing the pontiff's personal conduct, which was widely criticized even by his contemporaries.

itens.resumo: The "Warrior Pope" of the early sixteenth century, who launched the construction of the new Saint Peter's Basilica and commissioned Michelangelo to paint the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel.
itens.corpo: Giuliano della Rovere, elected in 1503, became known for personally leading military campaigns to consolidate the Papal States, which earned him the nickname "Warrior Pope." He was also one of the greatest artistic patrons in papal history: he commissioned Bramante to design the new Saint Peter's Basilica, begun in 1506, and Michelangelo to paint the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel (1508-1512) and his own tomb, of which the famous statue of Moses survives.

itens.resumo: Pope from the Medici family under whose pontificate Martin Luther was excommunicated, at the beginning of the Protestant Reformation.
itens.corpo: Giovanni de' Medici, elected pope in 1513, is remembered above all for the crisis that would mark his pontificate: in 1517 Martin Luther posted his ninety-five theses against the sale of indulgences in Wittenberg, beginning the Protestant Reformation. Leo X excommunicated Luther by the bull «Decet Romanum Pontificem» (1521), but the break was already irreversible. A great patron of the arts in the Medici family tradition, his pontificate is also associated with lavish spending that worsened the financial crisis of the Holy See.

itens.resumo: Pope who convened the Council of Trent in 1545 and approved the Society of Jesus, beginning the Catholic response to the Protestant Reformation.
itens.corpo: Alessandro Farnese, elected in 1534, is the transitional figure between the Renaissance papacy and the Counter-Reformation. In 1540 he formally approved the newly founded Society of Jesus, of Ignatius of Loyola, and in 1545 he finally convened the Council of Trent, postponed for decades amid European political tensions — a council that would respond doctrinally and disciplinarily to the Protestant Reformation over almost twenty years, under three successive pontificates.

itens.resumo: Dominican pope who brought the Council of Trent to a close, promulgated the Roman Missal of 1570, and organized the victorious coalition at the Battle of Lepanto.
itens.corpo: Antonio Ghislieri, a Dominican friar elected pope in 1566, devoted himself to implementing the reforms decided at Trent: he published the Roman Catechism (1566), the Breviary (1568) and the Roman Missal (1570), which unified the Latin liturgy for centuries. He organized the Holy League that defeated the Ottoman fleet at the Battle of Lepanto (1571), a victory he attributed to the intercession of the Rosary, and he subsequently instituted the feast of Our Lady of Victory (later, of the Rosary). He was canonized in 1712.
fontes: Saint Pius V, Bull «Quo Primum» (1570), promulgation of the Roman Missal

itens.resumo: Pope who introduced, in 1582, the Gregorian calendar now used civilly almost throughout the world.
itens.corpo: Ugo Boncompagni, elected in 1572, is remembered above all for the reform of the Julian calendar, which over the centuries had accumulated a drift of about ten days relative to the true solar year. The bull «Inter Gravissimas» (1582) suppressed those ten days and adjusted the rule for leap years, creating the Gregorian calendar, adopted first by Catholic countries and, gradually, by the whole world. He also founded several colleges for the formation of missionaries.

itens.resumo: Pope of the seventeenth century, under whose pontificate Saint Peter's Basilica was completed and the trial of Galileo Galilei took place.
itens.corpo: Maffeo Barberini, elected in 1623, presided over the final consecration of the new Saint Peter's Basilica in 1626, and commissioned Bernini to build the bronze baldachin over the main altar. His pontificate is also remembered for the trial brought by the Roman Inquisition against Galileo Galilei in 1633, for his defense of heliocentrism — a complex episode, with scientific, theological, and political dimensions, which the Church would recognize centuries later, under John Paul II, as a case of hasty judgment on the part of the theologians of the time.

itens.resumo: Pope who, under intense pressure from the European crowns, suppressed the Society of Jesus in 1773.
itens.corpo: Elected in 1769 amid strong pressure from the monarchies of Portugal, Spain and France — which had already expelled the Jesuits from their territories —, Clement XIV signed the brief «Dominus ac Redemptor» (1773), suppressing the Society of Jesus throughout the Catholic world, with the exception of territories such as Prussia and Russia, where non-Catholic or Orthodox rulers refused to publish the decree. The Order would be restored by Pius VII in 1814.

itens.resumo: Pope who faced the French Revolution and died a prisoner of the French troops in 1799.
itens.corpo: Elected in 1775, Giannangelo Braschi saw his pontificate dominated by the consequences of the French Revolution: the Civil Constitution of the Clergy (1790), which subordinated the Church in France to the State, and the subsequent French invasion of the Papal States. In 1798 Napoleon's troops occupied Rome and proclaimed a republic; the pope, already elderly and ill, was taken prisoner to France, where he died in Valence in August 1799.

itens.resumo: The pope who crowned Napoleon emperor in 1804 and later faced his own forced exile at the hands of the same emperor.
itens.corpo: Barnaba Chiaramonti, elected in 1800 amid the instability left by the French Revolution, signed the Concordat of 1801 with Napoleon, which reestablished Catholicism as the religion of the majority of the French people after years of revolutionary persecution. In 1804 he presided over the ceremony in which Napoleon was crowned emperor at Notre-Dame — although Napoleon himself placed the crown on his own head. Relations deteriorated in the following years: in 1809 Napoleon annexed the Papal States and exiled the pope, who would return to Rome only after the emperor's fall in 1814, restoring the Society of Jesus in that same year.

itens.resumo: Camaldolese pope of the early nineteenth century, a champion of the missionary impulse and a critic of the liberal movements of Europe.
itens.corpo: A Camaldolese monk elected pope in 1831, Gregory XVI devoted special attention to missionary expansion, creating dozens of new dioceses and vicariates apostolic in Asia, Africa and Oceania, and condemned the slave trade in the apostolic letter «In Supremo Apostolatus» (1839). Politically conservative, he opposed the liberal and nationalist movements that stirred Europe and the Papal States in his time.
fontes: Gregory XVI, Apostolic Letter «In Supremo Apostolatus» (1839)

itens.resumo: Pope with the longest pontificate in history (almost 32 years), who defined the dogma of the Immaculate Conception and convened the First Vatican Council.
itens.corpo: Giovanni Maria Mastai-Ferretti, elected in 1846, had the longest verified pontificate in the history of the Church. In 1854 he defined the dogma of the Immaculate Conception of Mary; in 1864 he published the "Syllabus of Errors" (Syllabus Errorum), a list of condemned propositions linked to the liberalism and rationalism of his time; and in 1869-1870 he convened the First Vatican Council, which defined the dogma of papal infallibility shortly before it was interrupted by the invasion of Rome by the troops of the Kingdom of Italy, which put an end to the Papal States as a territorial entity. He was beatified in 2000.

itens.resumo: Pope of the late nineteenth century, author of the encyclical «Rerum Novarum», the founding document of the Church's modern social doctrine.
itens.corpo: Vincenzo Gioacchino Pecci, elected in 1878, had one of the longest and most intellectually influential pontificates in recent history. In 1891 he published the encyclical «Rerum Novarum», on the condition of workers in industrial society — the founding text of modern Catholic social doctrine, which defends both private property and collaboration between classes, as well as the right to form trade unions and a just wage. He also promoted the revival of Thomistic studies with the encyclical «Aeterni Patris» (1879).

itens.resumo: Pope of the early twentieth century who lowered the age for First Communion and promoted liturgical and catechetical reforms.
itens.corpo: Giuseppe Sarto, elected in 1903, is remembered for his motto «Instaurare omnia in Christo» («To restore all things in Christ»). He lowered the recommended age for First Communion to the «age of reason» (around seven years old), encouraged frequent Communion among the faithful, and promoted the reform of the Breviary and of Gregorian chant. He opposed what he called theological «Modernism» in the encyclical «Pascendi Dominici Gregis» (1907). He died in 1914, days after the start of the First World War. He was canonized in 1954.

itens.resumo: Pope whose pontificate coincided almost entirely with the First World War, amid repeated appeals for peace.
itens.corpo: Giacomo della Chiesa, elected in 1914, days after the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand that set off the First World War, devoted a large part of his pontificate to appeals for peace and to humanitarian efforts — including a seven-point peace proposal in 1917, which the belligerent powers rejected. He promulgated the first Code of Canon Law in history, in 1917, and wrote the missionary encyclical «Maximum Illud» (1919).
fontes: Benedict XV, Code of Canon Law (1917)

itens.resumo: The Pope who signed the Lateran Treaty, creating Vatican City State, and instituted the feast of Christ the King.
itens.corpo: Achille Ratti, elected in 1922, resolved the so-called "Roman Question" by signing, in 1929, the Lateran Treaty with Mussolini's Italian government, which recognized the sovereignty of the tiny Vatican City State — a territorial solution that endures to this day. He instituted the liturgical feast of Christ the King (1925) and published encyclicals of strong social and political content, among them "Quadragesimo Anno" (1931, forty years after "Rerum Novarum") and "Mit brennender Sorge" (1937), condemning Nazism.
fontes: Pius XI, Encyclical Letter "Mit brennender Sorge" (1937)

itens.resumo: Pope whose pontificate spanned the Second World War; he defined the dogma of the Assumption of Our Lady in 1950.
itens.corpo: Eugenio Pacelli, elected in 1939, a few months before the outbreak of the Second World War, guided the Holy See through one of the most dramatic periods of the twentieth century. His conduct during the Holocaust — between discreet diplomacy and local actions to protect the persecuted, and public silence on certain episodes — remains the subject of historiographical debate. In 1950 he defined the dogma of the Assumption of Our Lady, body and soul, into Heaven, and in 1943 he published the encyclical «Divino Afflante Spiritu», opening the way for modern Catholic biblical studies.

itens.resumo: The "Good Pope," who convened the Second Vatican Council in 1962, although he did not live to see it concluded.
itens.corpo: Angelo Roncalli, elected in 1958 at the age of 76 and seen by many as a "transitional pope," surprised everyone by convoking, in 1959, an ecumenical council — Vatican II, opened in October 1962 — to promote what he called "aggiornamento" (updating) of the Church in the face of the contemporary world. He wrote the encyclicals "Mater et Magistra" (1961) and "Pacem in Terris" (1963), the latter published in the midst of the Cuban Missile Crisis. He died in June 1963, before the end of the council. He was canonized in 2014.
fontes: Saint John XXIII, Bull "Humanae Salutis" (1961), convoking the Second Vatican Council

itens.resumo: Pope who guided and brought to a close the Second Vatican Council, promulgating its liturgical reforms and the encyclical «Humanae Vitae».
itens.corpo: Giovanni Battista Montini, elected in 1963, continued the Second Vatican Council after the death of John XXIII, presiding over its last three sessions and promulgating the conciliar documents until its close in 1965. He implemented the post-conciliar liturgical reform, including the New Roman Missal (1969), and in 1968 published the encyclical «Humanae Vitae», reaffirming Catholic teaching on the regulation of birth amid intense public debate. He was the first pope of the modern era to travel extensively outside Italy. He was canonized in 2018.
fontes: Saint Paul VI, Encyclical Letter «Humanae Vitae» (1968)

itens.resumo: The "Smiling Pope," whose pontificate, the second shortest in modern history, lasted only 33 days, in 1978.
itens.corpo: Albino Luciani, elected in August 1978, chose the double name John Paul in honor of his two immediate predecessors, signaling continuity with the spirit of the Council. Known for his simple and affable style, he died suddenly on September 28 of the same year, after only 33 days of pontificate — one of the shortest in the history of the Church — which caused great grief and, for decades, unfounded speculation about the causes of his death, which historians today attribute to natural causes.

itens.resumo: Karol Wojtyła, pope from 1978 to 2005; he promulgated the Catechism of the Catholic Church and the 1983 Code of Canon Law.
itens.corpo:
Karol Wojtyła was born in Wadowice, Poland, in 1920. A priest and later Archbishop of Kraków, he took part in the Second Vatican Council. He was elected Bishop of Rome on October 16, 1978, the first non-Italian pope in several centuries.

His pontificate, one of the longest in history, was marked by apostolic journeys to every continent, by the institution of World Youth Days, and by an extensive magisterium, with encyclicals such as «Redemptor Hominis» (1979), «Veritatis Splendor» (1993) and «Fides et Ratio» (1998). He promulgated the Code of Canon Law in 1983 and the Catechism of the Catholic Church by the Apostolic Constitution «Fidei Depositum» in 1992.

He died on April 2, 2005. He was canonized on April 27, 2014 by Francis. His liturgical memorial is celebrated on October 22.
fontes: John Paul II, Apostolic Constitution «Fidei Depositum» (October 11, 1992)

itens.resumo: Joseph Ratzinger, pope from 2005 to 2013; he resigned from the Petrine ministry, an extremely rare case in the history of the Church.
itens.corpo:
Joseph Ratzinger was born in Marktl am Inn, in Bavaria (Germany), in 1927. A theologian and university professor, he took part in the Second Vatican Council as a peritus. He was Archbishop of Munich and Freising and, for many years, Prefect of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, a period in which he closely followed the drafting of the Catechism of the Catholic Church.

Elected Bishop of Rome on April 19, 2005, he wrote the encyclicals «Deus Caritas Est» (2005), «Spe Salvi» (2007) and «Caritas in Veritate» (2009), as well as the trilogy «Jesus of Nazareth». He convoked the Year of Faith and gave impetus to the theme of the relationship between faith and reason.

On February 11, 2013, he announced, through the «Declaratio», his resignation from the ministry of Bishop of Rome, effective February 28, 2013. He then lived as Pope emeritus in the Vatican and died on December 31, 2022.
fontes: Benedict XVI, Encyclical Letter «Deus Caritas Est» (December 25, 2005)

itens.resumo: Jorge Mario Bergoglio, the first Jesuit pope and the first from Latin America, elected in 2013 and died in 2025.
itens.corpo: Archbishop of Buenos Aires, the Argentine Jorge Mario Bergoglio was elected pope in March 2013, following the resignation of Benedict XVI, becoming the first Jesuit pope and the first born in the Americas. He chose the name Francis in reference to Saint Francis of Assisi, signaling a pastoral emphasis on simplicity and attention to the poor. He published encyclicals such as «Laudato Si'» (2015), on integral ecology, and «Fratelli Tutti» (2020), on human fraternity, and convened synods on the family and on synodality. He died in April 2025.

itens.resumo: Robert Francis Prevost, elected in May 2025, the first pope born in the United States.
itens.corpo: Robert Francis Prevost, an Augustinian religious with a long missionary career in Peru — where he also served as a bishop — and head of the Dicastery for Bishops in Rome, was elected pope in May 2025, succeeding Francis. He became the first pontiff born in the United States, taking the name Leo in reference, as he indicated publicly, to the social tradition of the Church inaugurated by Leo XIII with "Rerum Novarum." This collection records here only the beginning of his pontificate; his magisterium is still ongoing.

itens.resumo: Ninth-century Roman pope who supported the convocation of the Fourth Council of Constantinople and saw his own family murdered amid the political disputes of his time.
itens.corpo:
Born into a noble Roman family already linked to two earlier popes, Adrian was about 75 years old and was married — before being widowed and becoming a priest — when he was elected in December 867, succeeding Nicholas I. His pontificate continued his predecessor's policy of asserting Roman authority in the face of secular powers, in a context of serious tensions with the local nobility: his wife and his daughter, still living, were murdered by partisans of a rival claimant to Emperor Louis II.

With the support of Adrian II, the Byzantine emperor Basil I convened in Constantinople, between 869 and 870, the council that the Catholic Church recognizes as the eighth ecumenical council. The assembly deposed Patriarch Photius and restored Ignatius to the patriarchate of Constantinople, although the pope and the emperor were unable to reach an agreement on the ecclesiastical jurisdiction of Bulgaria, a friction that would continue to sour relations between Rome and Constantinople in the following decades.
fontes: Acts of the Fourth Council of Constantinople (869-870)

itens.resumo: Reforming pope of the 11th century whose legacy to Constantinople, in 1054, led to the mutual excommunication that tradition identifies as the beginning of the Great Schism of the East.
itens.corpo:
Bruno of Egisheim-Dagsburg, bishop of Toul in Lorraine before being elected pope in 1049, devoted his pontificate to combating simony — the buying and selling of ecclesiastical offices — and the concubinage of the clergy, personally traveling through France, Germany and Italy to preside over reform synods, something unusual for a pope of his time. He brought to Rome clerics who would become central figures of the reform of the Church in the following century, among them Humbert of Silva Candida and the monk Hildebrand, the future Pope Gregory VII.

In 1054, already near the end of his life, he sent to Constantinople a legation headed by Cardinal Humbert of Silva Candida to negotiate with Patriarch Michael Cerularius, who had closed Latin churches in the city and contested liturgical practices of the West. The negotiations failed, and Humbert laid on the altar of Hagia Sophia a bull of excommunication against the patriarch — an act of questionable legal validity, since Leo IX himself had died shortly before, in April of that year. The episode, followed by a reciprocal excommunication on the part of Cerularius, is traditionally pointed to as the landmark of the Schism between the Churches of Rome and Constantinople.
fontes: Correspondence between Humbert of Silva Candida and Michael Cerularius (1054)

itens.resumo: A 12th-century pope and jurist who convened the Third Lateran Council and confronted Emperor Frederick Barbarossa and King Henry II of England in the case of Thomas Becket.
itens.corpo:
Rolando Bandinelli, a professor of theology and canon law at Bologna before serving as papal chancellor, was elected in 1159 in a contested election by a faction favorable to Emperor Frederick Barbarossa, who supported a succession of rival antipopes throughout almost the entire pontificate of Alexander — who was therefore obliged to spend long periods in exile, away from Rome.

His pontificate was also marked by the conflict between King Henry II of England and the Archbishop of Canterbury, Thomas Becket, who was murdered in his cathedral in 1170; Alexander III canonized him as early as 1173 and, the following year, received the public penance of the English king. Finally reconciled with Frederick Barbarossa by the Peace of Venice (1177), he convened the Third Lateran Council (1179), which established the requirement of a two-thirds majority of the cardinals for the valid election of a pope — a norm that sought precisely to avoid schisms such as the one that had marked his own pontificate.
fontes: Acts of the Third Lateran Council (1179)

itens.resumo: Blessed hermit elected pope at about eighty years of age to end a two-year conclave; he resigned five months later, the first clear case of free resignation from the papacy.
itens.corpo:
Pietro Angelerio (or Pietro da Morrone), a hermit monk and founder of a Benedictine congregation that would bear his name — the Celestines —, had lived for decades in strict penance in the mountains of Abruzzo when, in July 1294, he was elected pope to put an end to a conclave that had been deadlocked for more than two years after the death of Nicholas IV. He accepted the election already in his eighties, with no experience whatsoever in ecclesiastical government.

Unable to cope with the administration of the Curia and feeling papal life to be an obstacle to his vocation of silence and prayer, Celestine V promulgated a decree formally recognizing the possibility of a pope resigning, and he himself resigned from the office on December 13, 1294, after little more than five months of pontificate — the most clearly documented case of free papal resignation before Benedict XVI, in 2013. His successor, Boniface VIII, fearing that he might become the instrument of an antipope, had him detained; Celestine died a prisoner in 1296. He was canonized in 1313 by Pope Clement V.
fontes: Bull of resignation of Celestine V (December 13, 1294)

itens.resumo: Second pope of the Avignon period, involved in a controversy with the Spiritual Franciscans over the poverty of Christ and, at the end of his life, in a theological dispute over the beatific vision.
itens.corpo:
Jacques Duèse, a French jurist elected in 1316, definitively established the papal residence in Avignon, France, reorganizing the financial and bureaucratic administration of the Church so as to centralize in Rome — or rather, in Avignon — the appointment of bishops and the collection of ecclesiastical taxes throughout Latin Christendom. He condemned as heretical the Franciscan "Spirituals" who maintained that Christ and the apostles had lived in absolute poverty, clashing with a large part of the Franciscan Order.

Toward the end of his life, between 1331 and 1332, John XXII argued in personal sermons — not in a solemn document of the magisterium — that the souls of the just, even after being purified, would not enjoy the beatific vision of God before the Last Judgment. The thesis provoked a strong reaction from theologians, including the University of Paris, and the pope himself publicly retracted it shortly before his death in 1334, acknowledging the traditional teaching. His successor, Benedict XII, would formally define the doctrine of the immediate beatific vision of the just.
fontes: John XXII, sermons on the beatific vision (1331-1332)
Benedict XIV, "Benedictus Deus" (1336), taking up the controversy

itens.resumo: Humanist pope of the Renaissance, author of the only autobiography ever written by a reigning pontiff; he died while trying to organize a crusade against the Ottoman Turks.
itens.corpo:
Enea Silvio Piccolomini, a renowned writer and diplomat before being ordained a priest at the age of 41, was elected pope in 1458. His main literary legacy was the «Commentarii», an autobiographical account of his own pontificate without parallel in papal history — no other reigning pope wrote comparable memoirs.

Faced with the fall of Constantinople to the Ottomans in 1453, Pius II made the organization of a European crusade against the Turks the great cause of his pontificate, convening a congress of European princes in Mantua in 1459 and officially proclaiming the crusade in 1460, without obtaining effective support from the Catholic powers. Determined to lead the expedition in person, he died in August 1464 in the port city of Ancona, waiting for the Venetian fleet that was to carry him into battle.

itens.resumo: Franciscan pope of the Renaissance who had the chapel that now bears his name — the Sistine Chapel — rebuilt, and who founded the Vatican Library along modern lines.
itens.corpo:
Francesco della Rovere, a Franciscan who rose to minister general of his order before being elected pope in 1471, turned Rome into one of the main artistic and intellectual centers of Renaissance Europe. Between 1473 and 1481 he had the palatine chapel of the Vatican rebuilt, renamed the Sistine Chapel in his honor, and between 1481 and 1483 he brought together painters such as Botticelli, Perugino, and Ghirlandaio to decorate it with frescoes on the life of Moses and of Christ — before Michelangelo painted its famous ceiling, already under Julius II. He also gave the Vatican Apostolic Library a stable organization and its own premises.

His pontificate also had a darker side: at the request of the Catholic Monarchs of Spain, he authorized the creation of the Spanish Inquisition (1478), directed chiefly against New Christians of Jewish origin, and he became involved in the so-called Pazzi Conspiracy against the Medici in Florence. Historiography likewise recognizes his strong nepotism in favor of his nephews, several of whom were raised to the cardinalate.
fontes: Bull «Exigit sincerae devotionis» (1478), establishing the Spanish Inquisition

itens.resumo: The only Dutch pope in history and the last non-Italian before John Paul II; he tried to reform the Curia in the face of the advance of the Protestant Reformation, but was unable to overcome internal resistance.
itens.corpo:
Adriaan Florenszoon Boeyens, a native of Utrecht, a theologian trained at Leuven and later tutor to the future Emperor Charles V, was elected pope in 1522 as a compromise candidate between rival factions in the conclave — the last non-Italian to occupy the See of Rome until the election of John Paul II in 1978.

Faced with the advance of Martin Luther in Germany, Adrian VI publicly acknowledged, before the Diet of Nuremberg, the responsibility of the Roman Curia itself for the abuses that fueled the revolt — a gesture of self-criticism rare among the popes of his time — and tried to impose reforms of discipline and simplicity of life on the Roman clergy. He met with strong resistance from the cardinals and the papal court, accustomed to the splendor of Renaissance Rome, and died in 1523, after little more than a year and eight months of pontificate, without time to consolidate any lasting reform.
fontes: Instruction of Adrian VI to the Diet of Nuremberg (1522)

itens.resumo: Pope of the Counter-Reformation who, as founder of the Roman Inquisition, promoted the first Index of Prohibited Books and hardened the repression of heresy.
itens.corpo:
Gian Pietro Carafa, a Neapolitan and founder of the Theatine order, had already been, together with Paul III, the main driving force behind the creation of the Holy Office — the Roman Inquisition — in 1542, before being elected pope in 1555. As pope, he imposed extreme rigor on the tribunal, pursuing suspects of heresy without sparing bishops or cardinals.

In 1559 he promulgated the first Index of Prohibited Books («Index Librorum Prohibitorum») of Roman scope, which completely banned the works of about 550 authors, in addition to individual titles — a list considered draconian even by contemporary Catholic theologians, such as the Jesuits Peter Canisius and Diego Laínez, and largely abandoned soon after his death, in 1559. He also reformed the discipline of the Roman clergy and confined the Jews of Rome to the city's first ghetto, a measure of intolerance that would negatively mark his pontificate in historical memory.

itens.resumo: Pope who reorganized the Roman Curia into congregations and was responsible for the urban redevelopment of Rome's great pilgrimage routes in the late sixteenth century.
itens.corpo:
Felice Peretti, a Franciscan of humble origins — his father worked as a farmer — was elected pope in 1585. In little more than five years of pontificate, he lastingly reorganized the central administration of the Church, dividing the Roman Curia into fifteen permanent congregations — nine for spiritual matters, six for the temporal government of the Papal States — and fixed the maximum number of cardinals at seventy, a structure that would remain in force, with adjustments, for centuries.

He restored public order in Rome with a firm hand against banditry and promoted a vast program of urban works: he opened new streets linking the city's seven pilgrimage churches, erected Egyptian obelisks in central squares — among them the one in Saint Peter's — and reorganized the papal finances, leaving at his death, in 1590, a papal treasury more robust than at any previous moment.

itens.resumo: Pope who formally protested against the Peace of Westphalia (1648) in the bull «Zelo Domus Dei», though his objection did not alter the new religious balance in Europe.
itens.corpo:
Giovanni Battista Pamphilj, a jurist and diplomat in the service of the Holy See in Naples, France and Spain before being elected pope in 1644, had a pontificate marked by the conclusion of the Thirty Years' War and by the peace treaties that ended it in Westphalia in 1648.

Opposing clauses of the treaties that recognized the legitimacy of Calvinism in territories of the Empire and permanently transferred to Protestant hands ecclesiastical property that had previously been Catholic, Innocent X published in November 1648 the bull «Zelo Domus Dei», declaring null and void the provisions of the Peace of Westphalia contrary to the Catholic religion. The protest, however, came too late and was practically ignored by the signatory powers, a clear sign that the popes had ceased to be decisive arbiters in relations among the European states.
